tonight.d: Four flutes, each as long as an eight-year-old, in a back room hung with felt so nothing rings. The front row keeps its knees tucked in, because the ends come within a hand of them.
Someone has found songs recorded in the old air, ages ago, and plays them on good speakers. Every voice sounds spoken through a blanket, and the children laugh at the low notes until they're shushed.
The {block} band marches the arcade at noon behind the slow trolley, and the arcade rings for a full second after every chord. The bass horn is coiled so long that it rides on the trolley.
Hardly anyone climbs the stairs, so a string quartet has taken a stairwell for its echo. Listeners sit on the steps above and below, and the cab lobby next door goes quiet to hear it.
On the top terrace, where a six-metre horn weighs almost nothing, a player sounds the start of {painter}'s dawn. The note reaches the floor a couple of seconds late and very thin.
Heliox needs organ pipes nearly twice as long, so the {block} organ fills a six-deck atrium. At noon the organist plays for whoever is eating lunch on the terraces.
Mill lager on tap and a fiddle band in the corner of the Mill Hall. Nobody knows where the tunes came from, and the people from {nb} at the next table insist {nb} wrote them.
The {block} youth ensemble plays its first concert of the year to neighbours who have heard every wrong note through the walls since rehearsals began. They clap anyway, loudest for the drummer.

At one in the morning the wash room on deck {deck} fills with people singing over the machines. The machines keep good time, the room is the warmest on the deck, and half the neighbours are on night shift anyway.

tonight.t: Try a flute before it goes
tonight.d: The flute school opens its test room once a week, and anyone may try a new flute before it goes to its owner. Most people manage a noise. One in twenty gets a note, and the makers chalk their name on the wall.
At eleven, as the lamps fade along {street}, a cellist plays from a doorway until the light is gone. It's the same piece every night, and it ends when the lamps do, to the second.
A piper plays the cab lobby at Ring {ring} as the morning glides come in. In heliox the drones stand nearly as tall as the piper, and commuters walk a little faster past them.
Music that came in by light from a raft across the Shade, played late for anyone still up. The newest piece left there eleven years ago, which in {drum} counts as the latest thing.
Thirty handbells, every one older than its ringer, rung in the atrium by a team that practises on {weekday}s. Each bell has a name painted inside, and none of the names belongs to anyone living.
A pianist plays the drum's best room, hung with felt three layers deep. Seats are auctioned and the rents go back to everyone, so the people who couldn't get in are paid a little for missing it.
After dinner each table at the hall sings one song, and the cook judges. The cook always picks the table that washed up.
The {block} choir rehearses with the doors open, and anyone may stand at the back and join the bass line. In heliox even the basses sound bright, and they're touchy about it.
Forty singers on the end-wall terraces sing {painter}'s dawn up from grey to gold. The painter works from a desk somewhere out of sight, so the choir follows the light, not a conductor.
Everyone in the deck {hdeck} choir is over ninety, and they rehearse at just over half a g. They say breathing is easier up there, and nobody from the Low decks has the nerve to argue.
Two choirs, one on each bank of the Hollow, sing a round across three kilometres of lamp-night. The far bank's answer arrives faint and five seconds late, which is the joke the round was written for.
Rehearsing for a wedding in {nb}, the {block} choir needs an audience that won't cry. Volunteers get tea and are asked to keep a straight face through the last verse.

Years ago this hall traded a round with a passing raft, and tonight the choir sings both halves: its own verse, then the answer that came back thirty-three minutes later, in voices that never breathed this air.
The night shift sings as it comes off at six, all the way down the long tiled corridor by the Vats. It isn't a performance, but a small crowd waits at the end of the corridor every morning anyway.
A children's choir sings the atrium lamps up at half past six. Half of them are still in pyjamas, and the youngest conducts with a spoon.
After eleven a choir that only sings in steam takes over the baths, because the tiles hold a chord for three seconds. There are no auditions, just a rule about not splashing the tenors.
The {drum} and {nb} choirs meet for their yearly sing-off, judged by three people from a drum neither of them likes. The scores go back {years} years and are read out before the first note.

Once a month a choir sings a single piece at the edge of the dim wood, and then everyone goes back to not talking. The woodwardens time it to the minute, and the silence afterwards is longer than the song.
Every {weekday} the {drum} choir sings at the Count board at Ring {ring} as the week's numbers change. This week the gap closed a little, and the choir went up a key.
Every leap at a third of a g lands a hand's width spinward, so a leaping reel walks itself round the terrace over an evening. By the last set the band has moved its chairs three times.
Couples dance on the Hollow's lawn after the dusk, at half a g, where a lifted partner takes half again as long to come down. The band plays slowly so nobody has to hurry a landing.
On {weekday} nights the neighbours on deck {deck} roll up the mats and dance the length of the corridor, the biggest room they have. People who can't fit dance in their doorways.
Aerial dancers perform in the netted flying hall, in wing-sleeves, at almost no weight at all. Their turns are slow and very long, and the crosswise drift is part of the choreography.
When the hall clears, the tables go against the walls and the reels start. Dancers who know the drum set off antispinward, where they weigh a little less and the jumps come easy.
On deck {hdeck} the elders waltz at just over half a g, where a turn costs nothing and a dip is very safe. The oldest couple is a hundred and eight and sits out nothing.
A dance at the wood's edge to music only the dancers can hear, through earpieces; the watchers hear feet on moss. At the end the watchers applaud with their hands in the air, without a sound.
When the last freight goes out, the stalls on the Quaysides fold away and a band plays for the night crews. They dance at a full g down there, and claim it makes them better at it.

tonight.t: New soles, tested at a reel
tonight.d: The cobblers' school tests its year's soles at a reel: forty dancers in forty new pairs, and three old cobblers on a bench listening for squeaks. A squeak means the pair goes back.
Couples dance on the end-wall terraces through {painter}'s dusk, and the band follows the light. When it goes blue they slow down; when it turns gold nobody can keep them still.

tonight.t: The Eleven Days, by hand lamp
tonight.d: A company plays the Eleven Days with every lamp off but the actors' hand lamps. The oldest people in the audience lived through it, and they're the ones laughing at the scenes on the stairs.
On {street}, a puppet show for the under-sevens in which the puppets keep dropping things. The audience shouts 'anti!' before each one lands, and is always right.
A comedy about a {drum} family at a wedding in {nb}, with two bottles of gin each and a sofa nobody can afford. Half the audience glided over from {nb} for it, and they laugh hardest.

tonight.t: A play forty years by light
tonight.d: Forty years ago this play left a raft across the Shade; tonight {drum} stages it for the first time. Nobody knows how the writer meant the ending, and an answer would take eighty years.

tonight.t: A play with the far bank behind it
tonight.d: The company plays on the Hollow floor as the dusk comes down, with the far bank three kilometres overhead for a backdrop. In the last act the lamps come on over there, exactly on cue.
A late play for the people who work the lamp-night: Yard crews, the laundry plant's engineers, the Gate's night staff. It's short and rude, and it starts exactly when it says.
Eight seats, two actors and a play about sharing a kitchen, performed in somebody's shared kitchen after the last dinner shift. Bring your own cup; there are only four.
Fourteen-year-olds wrote this one: a play about the year {drum} takes the Count down. It's very hopeful and a little long, and the parents are a mess by the end.
An afternoon play staged on a high deck for people who don't go down after dark. The cast came up by cab with the set, and the set is three chairs.
A mime company plays in the dim wood to an audience holding slates. Afterwards everyone writes a review and holds it up for the actors, who read them in silence and bow.
An opera in the great hall, lit like a dawn for the overture. Its tenor has the brightest voice in the {row} drums, which in heliox is saying something.

tonight.t: A letter nine years by light
tonight.d: A long letter has landed from a raft nine years away by light, and the hall reads it aloud. It was written to a man who has since died, so his table answers it, carefully, to be read once.
At the block court someone reads the year's {block} names: each newborn beside the dead whose share they carry. There are about twenty-five pairs, and people stand for the ones they knew.
A poet reads in the dim wood, barely above a whisper, which in heliox carries to the back row. Questions afterwards are written on slates and passed forward.
An aunt reads to the under-sevens on cushions after school. Adults may stay if they sit at the back and don't laugh at the voices.

tonight.t: A reading room for the sleepless
tonight.d: In a thin drum your bunk is someone else's until six, so the reading room on deck {deck} stays open all lamp-night. A reader reads aloud, very softly, to whoever is in the armchairs.
An elder reads on the terraces as the dawn comes up, a little louder each time the light brightens. By the last page you can see the far bank, and the elder can see the audience.

Last year's wanderers sent a card home from every row, and tonight the hall reads them in order, each with its light delay. The farthest came from thirty-six seconds away, and the room cheers it like a goal.
Anyone on guest-right is invited to read something from home at the hall tonight. Most guests read a recipe, and the cook takes notes.
Once a year {drum} reads its founding rules aloud, in turns, in the old hall by Ring {ring}. It takes all afternoon, and the clause about who may cut the Hollow's grass still gets a laugh.
Item one at the {block} court: a flute on deck {deck} that practises at midnight. The flautist plays a bar in defence, and the court settles on ten o'clock and a felt curtain.
Asked, again, to rule on which ring counter makes the best broth, the block court finds for Ring {ring}, as it has for {years} years. The losing side walks out laughing.
Bright atrium floor and grey terraces, or everything evenly dim? The block votes on its share of park light again, and the floor wins again, mostly because of the pear trees.
Somebody's starter crock has gone missing from the shared kitchen on {street}, and the court hears it out. It turns up before the vote, behind the rice, one spoon lighter, with a note saying sorry.

Half of tonight's block court is Hollow swaps: a lake morning for two orchard afternoons, a dusk for a dawn. You've been given an hour as a guest, and the whole court waits to see what you'll trade it for.
Since the vents were rebalanced, the far side of the block says its flats are cold and the near side has never been so comfortable. The court sends an engineer, lends out four blankets and moves on.
Nobody wants {weekday}s when the court redraws the hall's cooking rota. In the end the youngest table takes them, on condition that they choose the music.
Even the block court is silent in a wood drum: complaints come in on slates and are answered on slates. Tonight's is about someone's shoes, which squeak on the paths.

An apprentice wants the workshop lathe at night; the neighbours want to sleep. The court settles it in four minutes, lathe till ten, and the apprentice turns new feet for the court's bench by way of thanks.
Ramen on {weekday}s: one long table, four hundred seats, one cook. Guests on guest-right eat free and are expected to carry plates.

Jook from six at the Mill Hall, free from the commons, with chilli crisp and a bowl of the Nine on every table. Nobody under thirty admits to coming here by choice, and the queue is mostly under thirty.
Served in silence, the evening stew tastes better. Bowls come under lids, and lifting one is the loudest thing in the room.

The Blight Kitchen cooks what got {drum} through its bad years: blistered starch toasties, crackling 'steak', mock apple pie. The cooks are young and say they'll keep the menu when the Count comes down.
Mycelium steak in a dark sauce, Mill rice, and a side salad cut into four careful portions of three mouthfuls each. The salad is the treat; the pastry afterwards is the filler.
Volunteers wanted every afternoon, no experience needed: you chop, you carry, you eat last and best. The cook is seventy-eight and remembers last year's volunteers by name.
At six a hall in the Keel serves the shifts coming off: hot jook, vat egg, strong coffee under a lid. The Gate's night crew always takes the corner table and talks shop until seven.
Noon at the Mill Hall: cold glass noodles and starch jellies in chilli oil and black vinegar, with the Nine shaken over. 'Have some Nine,' says the woman at the hatch, to anyone who looks peaky.
Open kitchen night: anyone may cook one dish for the long table, and the table eats all of them. Tonight there are eleven kinds of dumpling and one salad, which goes first.
Four hundred seats, three thousand people: dinner runs in sittings by deck. Deck {deck} eats at seven tonight, and a guest may join any sitting with room.
In a thin drum the hall runs four sittings a night, and every seat is warm when you get it. The food is plain and generous, and the cook knows everyone's sitting by heart.
The craft school feeds its students at one long table, and anyone visiting the workshops may sit in. Every chair at it was made by a first-year, and you can tell which ones.
Gin is sold only in the halls after six, where someone is always cooking. It's cheap and has thiamine in it, and the cook pours it with a plate of something hot whether you asked or not.
After eleven the hall's hatch stays open for anyone coming in late: broth held below a simmer on the waste-heat loop, bread, and no questions. It's free, and it's always the same broth.
The halls here light their long tables like lamp-noon, just for lunch. When forty lids come off at once the steam shines, and the whole table goes 'oh' as if it were a show.
Bakers start at five, and the first loaves are out as the lamps come up. Guests may help knead in return for a heel, which is the best part and everyone knows it.
At nine the paddles at the far end of the lake start up, and the first wave takes a few minutes to reach the jetty. Boards are free; standing up on one is not.

tonight.t: Learn to stand on a wave
tonight.d: A swell teacher on the jetty takes beginners in fours. At half a g you fall off very slowly, which leaves time to wave at the teacher on the way down.
Elders have the first swell hour, floating on their backs in the lamp-dawn and letting the waves lift them. A wave at half a g lifts you so slowly you could fall asleep, and two of them do.
This morning the paddles run through {painter}'s dawn, so the waves come in rose, then gold. Half the lake is boarders and the other half came for the light and got wet.
Swell hours are auctioned here, so a guest can buy one. Two kays gets you a board, a wetsuit with someone else's name inked in the collar, and the biggest waves of the day.
On {weekday}s the paddles run into the dusk, and the last waves come in dark blue as the sunline fades. Boarders paddle out in a line with hand lamps clipped to their boards.

At the end of the dusk the sunline dims enough to fly beside, and the whole Spindle opens. Hand lamps go up from both end walls, and by ten the axis is a line of slow lights nearly four kilometres long.
A nine-year-old teaches crosswise flying in the netted hall: aim wide, the drum turns under you, and you'll come out somewhere else. Grown-ups pay a kay for the lesson; the laughing is free.

tonight.t: Sleeve hire at the flying hall
tonight.d: Wing-sleeves for hire at the back flying hall's gate, a few tenths of a kay. Along the axis you fly true; across it, the nets are there for a reason.
A choir flies the Spindle tonight with hand lamps, singing as it goes. From the floor you can't make out the words, only a bright thread of sound moving along the axis at walking pace.
Lengthwise races down the axis in the lamp-night, end wall to end wall. The fastest flyers do it in under ten minutes, and the slowest get the loudest cheer at the far net.
Toddlers learn to fly in the flying hall's padded corner, in sleeves no longer than an arm. They take to it faster than walking, while their parents hold on to the net and fret.
A guide takes guests up the Spindle lift and flies them a kilometre down the axis in the dark. The sunline is a dark cable beside you, and the Hollow's path lamps circle you on every side.

tonight.t: An afternoon in the flying hall
tonight.d: Anyone with sleeves may use the front flying hall this afternoon. Children play tag in three dimensions, and the adults fly lengthwise, carefully, like people who've hit the net before.
A club flies the length of the Spindle and back every {weekday} at midnight, lamps on their wrists, saying almost nothing. They're always down before the laundry starts.
At dusk the sleeve makers fly-test the day's work, and visitors may try a pair before it's delivered. The makers watch from the net with notebooks and say 'hm' a great deal.
An elders' hour in the lamp-night Spindle: slow lengthwise flights, nothing crosswise, and tea at the far net. Some of them haven't flown since their wander year and fly better than anyone.
{painter} has spent a year on this morning's dawn, and nobody knows how it starts. The terraces fill from five, and the coffee cart sets up wherever the painter's friends are sitting.

tonight.t: A dusk that ends in green
tonight.d: Seats on the end-wall terraces are auctioned for tonight's painted dusk, and the rents are shared out. The last forty minutes are green, and the terraces have been asked not to clap until it's over.
A first-year lamp-painter has the Hollow for a quiet {weekday} dawn, the kind nobody books. It's too pink and too fast, and the forty people who came stand up and clap anyway.
For a painted dawn, the best seat is the top terrace, where the light comes across the whole Hollow at once. At a twentieth of a g you can perch on the rail, and everyone does.
Painters play a dawn composed {years} years ago by someone long dead, exactly as written. A few elders say it was better the first time, which is what the elders said the first time too.
A painter has made tonight's dusk for a friend who died, in the friend's colours: amber, then a long slate grey. The terraces are full of people who never met either of them.
Before the dawn, a lamp-painter shows a dozen students the desk: three hours of sunline, thousands of lamps on the land, and one rule, which is that you play it once.
Every seat on the back terraces went at auction for {painter}'s dawn. Standing room on the floor is free and, some say, better.
Wood-drum painters work low: their dusks are mostly greys, with a single minute of copper at the end. For that minute the yews look like old bronze, and nobody under them moves.
A couple has asked a painter for their wedding dusk, which the whole Hollow gets to see. It's gold all the way down, which the painter calls unsubtle and the couple calls perfect.

tonight.t: A guest's hour at the lake
tonight.d: Guests get one Hollow hour, and most spend it at the lake. A dive off the jetty takes half again as long to fall, and everyone comes up laughing at how long they were in the air.
By allotment the lake belongs to the elders at lamp-dawn. Guests may swim at the far end if they're quiet, and the elders will tell them, kindly, that they aren't.
Lake hours are auctioned here, and the late ones go cheap: about two kays for an hour. The lake is part of the drum's water reserve, and the lifeguard asks you not to splash too much of it out.

tonight.t: A swim under the far bank
tonight.d: At half a g a splash goes up twice as high and takes its time coming down. Out in the middle of the lake you can float and look straight up at the far bank, where people are picnicking upside down.
From the jetty's high board, at half a g, the drop takes nearly a second and a half. Children go off it in pairs, holding hands, and shout the whole way down.
A swim club does lengths through the whole three-hour lamp-dawn, while the water turns from grey to gold. Visitors may join for the last lap, which is the brightest.
After the dusk the lake stays open with lamps under the water, so every swimmer is a dark shape in green glass. It's the drum's oldest late-night date, and it's always crowded.

In a thin drum the Hollow hours are short and the lake is full; tonight it's {block}'s turn. Everyone floats shoulder to shoulder and watches the far bank's lamps come on overhead, one district at a time.
Lessons in the shallows before the Hollow fills, where a child at half a g can jump and come down slowly enough to learn how. The teacher stands waist-deep and catches everyone.
You've won an afternoon at the lake in the drum's Hollow lottery. The water is warm, crowded and full of people who also can't believe their luck.

After the last freight the Quaysides fill with stalls: produce from {nb}'s racks, noodles at about a kay a bowl, and a stall that sells nothing but lids. It packs up at two, when the Yard crews go back.
Things too good to recycle and too big to keep, laid out down the corridor: everything traded, nothing bought. The best thing on the tables tonight is a chair with four owners' mends.
Half a kay each, laid out under glass like rings: the greengrocer's new case of tomatoes, in this morning from {nb}. People come to look as much as to buy.
Bring a coat, take a lining: the tailors on {street} run a swap of offcuts in this year's colours. A sleeve's worth of hard algae blue goes for a strip of old ochre and a story.
Crates from {nb}'s Garden racks come in on the first glide trains of the morning, and the market at Ring {ring} gets first pick. By seven the strawberries are gone and the arguing has started.
Old wing-sleeves, mended and remade, some with three or four owners' initials inked inside the cuff. A good pair costs less than a new shirt and flies better than a new pair.
You'll want a sprig for your host: cuttings from a hundred herb shelves, three hundredths of a kay each. It's the oldest manners there are, and the stallholders will tell you which herbs travel.
Lit as bright as the Hollow at lamp-noon, the arcade market shows every colour true, which is why dyers glide in from three drums away to choose here. Nobody else would spend the light.
Starter crocks change hands at the night market, every one registered with the strain library. A spoon of a ninety-year-old rye starter goes for a spoon of anything new, which is the whole point.
Market day at Ring {ring}, under the Count board. The stalls are thin on luxuries and thick on mending, and the fruit seller gives every child a strawberry, which she says is policy, not kindness.
Hard bread, aged cheese, miso, dried noodles and tins of the Nine, sold by the people who made them. Every larder could do with something, and every stallholder says theirs keeps longest.
Spirits are taxed hard here, and the market posts the warnings: never gin from a stranger's bottle. The licensed stall at the end charges a price that makes visitors from {nb} laugh out loud.
Quayside bakers open at five for the night crews, and the queue for the first sourdough reaches the platform. A heel costs almost nothing; a whole loaf, still warm, a little more.
Dye makers sell colours by the gram at the night market, which is how a drum's fashions start. A pinch of this year's red costs less than a coffee and changes a coat entirely.
League night in the school's long hall: a ball thrown spinward dives, one thrown anti sails, and the small players throw anti. The visiting team from {nb} has never once won here.
No hall is free, so deck {deck} plays spinball down its main corridor with the doors shut. Every throw breaks by its heading, the corridor is two metres wide, and the score is mostly apologies.
Children race antispinward down the arcade, where they're lightest, and lose every rematch run the other way. Parents hold the tape and bet in Hollow minutes.

tonight.t: High jump at a third of a g
tonight.d: High jump on the terraces, where a good jumper clears four metres and comes down most of a metre spinward of where they aimed. The bar is a ribbon, and the landing mat is mostly for show.
Both drums glide to the {drum} and {nb} spinball final. Half the crowd comes over on the evening trains, and the ring counter runs out of rice balls by half-time.
Racers climb the end wall from the floor to the top terrace, getting lighter at every tier. The first half is the hard part; over the last terraces they could almost float.
Spinball for the over-seventies on deck {hdeck}, where the ball breaks gently and the players argue every call. The referee is ninety-four and has been wrong since before most of them were born.
A running club laps the rim deck in the lamp-night, almost nineteen kilometres round at a full g. They run spinward because it's harder, and mention it at breakfast as if it were a virtue.
Football on the third-g terrace: a long kick sails if it's going anti and dives if it's going spin. The teams change ends at half-time and argue about it at full time.
Wing-sleeve races in the netted hall, each racer in sleeves they made this year. The course goes crosswise twice, and the makers lose as often as anyone.
Every {weekday} for {years} years the Gate has played the Mill at spinball, and the Gate has won slightly more. Visitors may join either side, and the Mill always asks first.

tonight.t: Noodle pulling at a third of a g
tonight.d: A cook teaches noodle pulling on the third-g terrace, where a strand can hang three times as long before it tears. Beginners' strands break at about two metres, and the teacher eats the pieces.
Bring something torn to the tailor's on {street} and leave with the tear shown off. The teacher's own coat carries seven owners' mends, and the class is allowed to read them.
Care of a crock, taught at the starter school: feed it, keep it warm, register it with the strain library, and never lend it to a cousin. Everyone leaves with a spoon of the house mother.
An hour with a flute teacher, on flutes so long a child needs both hands just to hold one level. First lessons are mostly about breathing, and partly about not hitting the person next to you.

Visitors may use the chair school's benches tonight: cut one joint by hand and glue it into a chair a student will finish next month. Somewhere in {drum} are chairs with a hundred strangers' joints in them.
A short class for travellers on table manners: lids on everything, lift yours when it reaches you, never leave a dish bare. The teacher claims to read your upbringing from one uncovered bowl.
Children paint a dawn for their own atrium: an hour at a practice desk and one go at the real lamps tomorrow at half past six. Every one of them chooses purple.
Brushes out: the school's youngest class is dabbing the pear blossom in the atrium one flower at a time. Visitors may help if they promise to be gentle and not to sneeze.
Before the Hollow opens, an instructor takes beginners round the flying hall in the half-light: sleeves on, arms wide, follow the axis. At this hour nobody minds you hitting the net.
Open day at the Gate on Ring {ring}: the sequencer bay, how a crate is spot-checked, how a yogurt's genome is read, how a famine is stopped in a long room with clean benches.
A dyer shows how to re-dye a coat for under a tenth of a kay. The class does scarves first; most come out a brown nobody planned, which the dyer calls the colour of beginners.
A woodwarden takes six people through the dim wood for an hour, saying nothing, pointing with a long pruning hook. By the end you notice the yews have been cut so the light falls on the paths.
Lessons for adults who never learnt as children: axis flies true, spin sinks, anti floats. Each adult is put in a team with three children, who explain the rules again, slowly, after every throw.
The hall's cook teaches jook at five, before the lamps come up: rice, water, a lot of stirring and some patience. You eat what you make, and the cook's own pot sits on the next table for comparison.
The child's table stands up in the {block} atrium, two parents and four aunts, and both names are read: the child's and the dead's. The dead's family has brought a remade cradle.
At the Ledger hall a new name goes up beside an old one, and both families are there. The dead man's daughter holds the baby first, which is the custom, and takes a long time to hand it back.
Guests are welcome at the back of tonight's naming. The child is named for a lift engineer from deck {deck}, and the engineer's old crew has come in their work jackets.
In a wood drum a naming is silent: the child's table stands, the two names are written on a slate and held up, and the slate is kept. Babies don't know the rule and say plenty.
Tonight's naming gift from the dead man's family is his chair, remade by a maker who knew him, with new feet and the old seat. It's far too big for the child, which is the point.
A naming for a family's third child, rare enough that half the deck turns up. Nobody here fines a third; they just bring more cake.
A naming at the Mill Hall for a child named after a teacher who died last year, with the teacher's old class in the front rows. They're forty now and still can't sit still.
Short vows on the third-g terrace, then the officiant cuts an orchard apple crosswise and holds up the halves. For most of the guests it's the only star they'll ever see, and they lean in.

tonight.t: A wedding with room at the end
tonight.d: Room for wanderers at the far end of the table: the hall is hosting a wedding. You'll be asked to dance the reel, and the apples come round cut crosswise, one star for every two guests.
A couple of twenty marry in the atrium this afternoon and go home to a Margin flat lent by the drum. Their table gives them a sofa remade from three old ones, which is mostly the springs of one.
Vows under the yews, written on slates and shown, not spoken. When the apple is cut and the star held up, the only sound is the guests breathing in.
The wedding hall is lit like lamp-noon until midnight, the drum's gift to any couple who asks. The other gifts are Hollow hours bought at auction, and the bride's family has bought a great many.
Guests from {nb} have brought their two bottles each to tonight's wedding, and the hosts pretend not to have been looking forward to it. The cake is Mill sugar, four tiers high.
A wedding in a corridor, because it's the only room big enough. Neighbours lend chairs from their own kitchens so nothing matches, and the first dance goes down the middle between two rows of doors.

tonight.t: The cook's stew, one last time
tonight.d: Forty years this cook fed the block, and tonight the hall holds her memorial. Everyone eats her stew from the recipe on the wall, and her share goes back to the drum for a child not yet born.

The back crews hold a memorial for one of their own: forty years on the panels, and her crew patch on the table, stitched with a band of tiny stars. Old hands tell what she saw; the young listen as if at a Window.
In their mother's memory, a family has asked the painter for a dawn and invited anyone who's up. It's a slow one: grey for an hour, then gold all at once.
On the anniversary of the Eleven Days, elders who lived through it sit in the dark at lamp-dawn for eleven minutes, one for each day. Then the lamps come up and someone puts the kettle on.
Under the orchard trees she kept for sixty years, the block remembers a woodwarden. Her apprentice reads out everything she planted, which takes a while, and nobody minds.
An elder died with no family left, so the block holds the memorial and anyone may come. When a child is born into the share, the yearly note will go to the block instead.
She stopped a blight at the Gate in her twenties, which is why {drum} still eats well, and today the drum says goodbye. The Count board at Ring {ring} goes dark for a minute, which it never does.
Water from the food plant's waste-heat loop, hot for free; only the pumping costs. In heliox it's the cheapest luxury in the drum, and the steam room is where the gossip lives.
Half the teenagers in the baths wear a black thread round the left wrist: gone dark, saving for something, here because it's warm, free and full of people. Ask what they're saving for.
At six the baths are full of children being washed before school, at speed, by parents who have done it a thousand times. The water is at its hottest and the noise is tremendous.
Baths run in shifts like everything else in a thin drum, and deck {deck} has ten o'clock tonight. Bring a towel, take a number, and expect to share the pool with someone's grandmother.
In a wood drum even the baths are silent, which in a room of tile and steam takes effort. You can hear the water moving in the pipes behind the walls.
The baths stay open till two for anyone coming off a late glide. The attendant keeps a pot of tea on the waste-heat loop and asks where you've come from.
Lit like lamp-noon and tiled in colours that cost nothing and look like they cost everything. Entry is a few tenths of a kay, and the attendants wear white, which nobody else in the drum would dare.
Beside the hot pools is one kept cold, and in heliox cold is very cold. The custom is to get in, say something rude, and get straight out again.
Elders have the baths to themselves at lamp-dawn, when the water is cleanest and the room is quiet. They talk about the old days, which in the baths means last week.
Once the bread is in, the hall's bakers take the baths at half past five, flour and all. Guests who helped knead are invited, and somebody always brings the first loaf in a cloth.

Tonight the block makes larder together: hard bread in the slow ovens, cheese waxed, miso packed down, every jar labelled with the year. Guests get a jar of their own to take on, an honour and quite heavy.
Every household's larder is a matter of pride, and tonight the grandparents of {block} go round with notebooks. The prize is nothing at all, and people take it very seriously.
Pickling takes over the hall's kitchen: cucumbers from the racks, chillies, a whole crate of cabbage someone traded for. The deck smells sour for days, and every larder on it gets a jar.
On deck {deck} people trade what their larders have too much of for what they lack: three tins of the Nine for a block of hard cheese. In a thin drum every larder is small and every one is full.

Dried noodles for the larder: a noodle maker shows the block how, hanging them in the warm air of the Keel's drying room. They hang for a week, and visitors may hang one strand each with a name tag on it.
Its blight years taught {drum} to keep a deep larder, and tonight the Blight Kitchen's cooks show how. Everything keeps, nothing is wasted, and the mock apple pie keeps longest of all.

tonight.t: An evening with an old crew hand
tonight.d: Forty years on the radiator sleds, and now she talks about the stars to a room that has mostly never seen them. Asked what the River looks like, she thinks for a long time and says, 'Crowded.'

Every express is stored air, says tonight's speaker at the hall, and that's why Merrow has run its cyclers fast since the Eleven Days. The speaker was nineteen at the time and still keeps two larders.
Questions for the Gate, answered at Ring {ring}: why your seeds were held, what a prophage is, why the yogurt you carried in will be yours again in a week. It's the busiest talk on the platform.

A steward walks visitors through the Ledger: the Margin, tonight's guests, and why the Margin never goes to births. Councillors from a counted drum along the row sit at the back and write it all down.
Two old friends, one from {drum} and one from {nb}, argue in public about where a drum should sit on the gin curve. It ends where it always does, with both of them drinking the cheaper gin.
In the wood a talk is a slate passed round a circle: one question at the top, everyone adds a line. Tonight's question is 'What did you hear today?', and the slate goes round twice.
After the last sitting the hall keeps its lamps half up for anyone who wants to talk. Tonight it's a table of strangers on whether the beam will be flat this year, which it nearly always is.

tonight.t: Ten minutes at the coffee cart
tonight.d: Every {weekday} at dawn the coffee cart on the back terraces has a speaker while the light comes up: ten minutes on anything. This week it's a lift engineer on why the cabs lean.
How do you rehearse for a thirty-three-minute wait? A choir-master who sang to the last passing raft explains, and the answer involves a lot of tea and not looking at the clock.

tonight.t: An open meeting on the Count
tonight.d: An open meeting in the hall about the Count: how far {drum} is from par, and how many years it will take. Nobody shouts, everyone has a chart, and the tea is excellent.

New guests at Ring {ring} get the steward's short talk: where the Margin flats are, when the halls eat, how to leave a flat, and that herbs, not gin, are the host gift. It's three minutes long and well practised.
The block meets in the corridor because the hot-bunk rota has broken again: three people swapped shifts at once. A chart goes up on a door in chalk, and by ten it works.

The hall plays a slow world against a team in the {farrow} drums, on the big screen, with a few seconds' wait after every move. Nobody watching minds the wait, because that's when the shouting happens.

Neighbouring drums are close enough to play without lag, so {drum} and {nb} share a world every {weekday}. Tonight's game is a city that has been building for {years} years and has its own historians.

tonight.t: Slow chess with the far side
tonight.d: Slow chess against a hall on the far side of Merrow, played by the whole room: one move a night, voted on, sent by light. The game is in its third year and the hall is losing.
The shared room on deck {deck} runs a world on one old screen for whoever's awake. Twelve people play a single character and argue about every door.
{drum}'s young people play a slow world against the open drums of the row, and win more than their share. They say a long stop teaches you patience.
On deck {hdeck} the elders run a slow world with a seven-second wait built in on purpose. They say it's fair to players on the far side; really it's so nobody has to hurry.

tonight.t: A spare couch at the Window
tonight.d: This afternoon's round at the Window has a spare couch among a hundred and forty children and their grown-ups. Guests may take it if they promise not to talk through the twenty minutes of waiting in the red light.

Every child here goes to a Window once, at about eight, with one grown-up of their choosing. A girl's grandmother is unwell, and the girl has decided, very firmly, that the traveller next door will do instead.
Guests go to the Window by lottery, one couch a round, and your name has come up. The way there is the Spindle lift, the back axle and an armoured car, and the guide says to eat first.

tonight.t: The River again, before the end
tonight.d: Elders who went once at eight and want to see the River again have a round at the Window today. They talk through the twenty minutes of waiting and go silent when the shutter opens.
A raft's edge is due to cross a bright orange star this afternoon, and a Window has opened an extra round to watch it. It takes most of an hour, and the old back-crew hands are taking bets.

tonight.t: A crew hand for a guide
tonight.d: Today's guide at the Window spent thirty years on the radiator crews and knows every black shape in the sky by its raft's name. One of them, she says, is the raft we sent our songs to.

arrive.t: Twenty past five, and the platform belongs to the Gate's night crew going off shift, a slow line of them with their hoods down. One holds the cab core's door for you without opening her eyes.
At this hour the ring counter's hatch is only half up, and the cook ducks under it to hand you a cup. The broth is peppery enough to make your eyes water, which may be the point at half past five.
Your bag was a reasonable bag at home. At the rim, a full g, it seems to have packed something extra while you weren't looking.
Nobody told the Keel it was dawn. The platform lamps are as bright at half past five as at noon, and only the people tell you the time, yawning into their collars.

Freight comes in before people do. Crates of {nb}'s cherry tomatoes roll past on a trolley, each one sealed and stamped, and a Gate worker opens one in fifty with the face of someone choosing a sweet.

One old man stands at the front of the platform with his hand lamp switched on, though the platform is lit. He's an hour early for a wanderer coming home from {far}, and the counter cook keeps bringing him broth.
The first commuters stand exactly where the doors will open, holding cups, not talking. In an hour this platform will be loud; at a quarter to six it has the manners of a library.
A sign by the doors asks for quiet, and the platform obeys. Two commuters pass a slate back and forth over their broth, and the loudest thing on Ring {ring} is the counter's hatch going up.

The Count hangs over the ring counter in plain white figures: people on one line, places on the next, the gap between them a little narrower than last month. Nobody stops to read it. They've all read it.

Before the shops open, the apprentices are already in them, sweeping and sorting, and every window holds one example of the thing this drum is famous for, with a card saying who made it and who taught them.
Even the station ring is lit like a stage here. At this hour the ceiling runs a warm gold along the platform as if it had been composed, and a man on the night shift says it was.

Someone at the Ring {ring} hall is already cooking, and you can smell the jook pot and something with ginger from the platform. A sign on the hall door says guests eat free and are expected to carry plates.

At six the platform is already full, people coming off night work and people going on to it, passing like a relay. A man holds your bag while you read the bunk rota, then hands it back with a nod, as if this is a thing people do here. It is.
No names on the board here, just a plain register: people, places, guests, the hour. A man with a mop tells you the Mill Hall is two decks up on {street} and the jook is better than it looks.
A cleaning robot works its way along the platform edge at the pace of a slow walk, polishing out the night. It stops for your feet and waits until you move them.
Behind you the glide car sits at the jacket's inner face, its aft windows showing nothing but a metre of water with the platform lamps bent in it.
Out in the Quaysides the market is still trestles and folded cloths. A woman unwraps a tray of strawberries from {nb2} as carefully as if they were rings.

Over the cab core a sign gives the times up: Low decks under half a minute, Middle about a minute, the Hollow a minute and a half. You came from {nb} in two minutes twenty, which suddenly seems a long way.
A child in pyjamas is asleep across three seats with a parent's coat over her. The counter cook has put a rice ball by her hand for when she wakes.
Beside the guest desk is a list of {block} tables with a spare seat for dinner tonight. You pick one because it's in a child's handwriting, and all it says is: we have noodles.

The weight that came back at the catch stays. Your knees notice first, then your shoulders, then the strap of your bag, and by the counter you're walking like everyone else at the rim: flat-footed and in no hurry.
Two Gate workers going off shift are arguing about whose ring counter is better, theirs or the one at {nb}. It's a quarter to six and they've clearly been at it all night.
An old woodwarden on the platform writes on a slate for a boy who has just arrived: WALK SLOWLY. EVERYTHING CARRIES. He reads it twice and takes off his shoes.
Next to the Count is a smaller board, older, with one line on it: anyone may glide out of this drum on any day. The paint is fresh. Someone keeps it that way.
First train in, and the counter has made too many rice balls. The cook presses two on you and a third for the road, then thinks better of it and keeps the third for the freight crew.
By midday the Quaysides are a market with a platform in it. You step off into a crowd haggling over herb cuttings, and somebody holds a sprig of mint under your nose to win an argument.
The Gate wants your starter crock before it wants you. A woman in a clean coat swabs it, reads the strain off her screen and hands it back with a sticker: registered at home, still itself.
A school group waits for the car you came on: forty children in a double line, a teacher at each end counting them twice. They're going one glide over to {nb2} to see a chair.

Notices round the station ring say what's on: a painted dusk tonight by {painter}, swell hour on the lake, a puppet play on the terraces. Underneath, smaller, is last year's returned rents, so much a head, which is the line people actually read.

There's a hall right on the platform with its doors open, and the noise comes out to meet you: four hundred people at lunch in a room that rings. A cook waves you in with a ladle before you've put your bag down.
Today's broth at the ring counter has a sprig of something green floating in it. The man ahead of you asks what it is, and the cook says, 'Ask the hall. They cut it.'
A freight crew is loading crates of strawberries for the trip back, every crate sealed and every seal stamped by two Gates. They carry them the way other people carry a sleeping baby.
This platform is plain and well kept, the sort of place that mends a bench instead of replacing it. Every third bench has a new slat in a slightly different colour.
A man in a good jacket is having two bottles of gin counted at a desk by the exit. Two is the allowance, he has two, and everyone involved looks faintly disappointed.

On the pillar by the cab core, in red, a poster shows what methanol-cut gin looks like and where the nearest clinic is. Under it someone has stuck a smaller note: or glide next door and bring back your two bottles.
Ring {ring} is long enough that its floor rises away in both directions, spinward and anti, until the ceiling cuts it off. Somewhere round that curve is the cab core you want.

The platform is crowded the whole way along, but nobody shoves; people turn sideways as a matter of course, the way you step round furniture at home. An old man offers you half his bench and most of his opinions.
One shop by the platform sells nothing but flutes, each about as long as a child is tall, hung on the wall in order of pitch. A girl is trying one, and the whole Quayside stops for her scale.

Wing-sleeves hang in the first shop off the platform, the remade pairs with their old owners' names stitched inside the cuffs. A notice offers lessons in crosswise flying, taught by nine-year-olds, most afternoons.
The station ring here is lit low and hung with felt, and the departures come up on a board instead of a voice. People pass with slates under their arms and nod instead of saying hello.

Midday at the Gate is a queue of people holding jars: yogurt, starter, a basil cutting wrapped in damp cloth, a crock somebody's great-grandmother kept. Each gets a swab and a number, and nobody minds, because everyone here has heard of a blight.
You step off into the smell of the Quaysides: brine from the pickle stalls, warm sugar, cold metal and broth. Your nose files it under new drum before the rest of you catches up.

Beside the Count is a door marked Clinic: Fittings, with a bench outside that nobody sits on. The rest of the platform is ordinary: broth, rice balls, a timetable and two old men disagreeing about it.
Children stand in front of a Ledger the size of a wall, doing sums out loud: births, deaths, Margin. Their teacher lets them argue until somebody gets it right.

A wedding party gets off the car behind you in their altered best, carrying a chair in a padded bag between two of them like a patient. They ask you the way to the Spindle lifts, and you have to admit you've been here four minutes.

The queue at the cab core has a rhythm: six in, doors shut, next six step up. You share a cab with a grandmother, a crate of tomatoes and a boy going up for his first flying lesson, and the cabin leans as it climbs.
One wall of the platform plays last night's painted dusk at a tenth of its brightness, with {painter}'s name in the corner. People stop to watch the ending, then catch their cabs.
Sweet, almost a pudding: that's this drum's broth. The woman beside you calls it a scandal and drinks two cups.
A choir is rehearsing in the station hall with the doors open, and the platform has stopped to listen without admitting it. In heliox the high voices come out bright as wire.
You came in on the noon train with a crate of {nb}'s tomatoes belted into the seat beside you. The freight man who unbuckles it thanks you for keeping it company.
Evening peak, and the platform is full of commuters coming home from a day one glide over. You're the only one walking against them, and a dozen people step aside for you without looking up.

The hall at Ring {ring} is serving dinner by the time you're off the car: stew in lidded pots down a table as long as the platform. A cook asks if you're a guest, sets a place, and says the stew is better if you don't ask what's in it.
Most of the queue at the ring counter is just off work, and the cook knows them by their order. You get a cup, a rice ball and a look that says you'll have an order of your own by the third night.
In the evening the Ledger shows its guests line in big figures, ticking up as each car empties. Yours makes it go up by one, and a boy who was watching says 'That's you' and goes back to his noodles.

The whole of {block} seems to have come down to meet a wanderer, and the platform is full of hand lamps and aunts. Nobody's sure which car the wanderer is on, so they cheer every car, including yours.
The Quaysides market is packing up, and prices fall with the shutters. A stallholder sells you a split tomato for a fifth of a kay and swears the split ones are sweeter.
A hundred people get off your train without a sound. A woman by the door holds up a slate that says WELCOME, then turns it over: KEEP YOUR VOICE DOWN.
Everybody gets off at once and the platform takes it, the way a full room takes one more chair. A woman hands you a bowl of noodles from the pot she's carrying to her shift and says you can owe her.
Out of rice balls, says the counter cook, and apologises as if it were a death in the family. The broth, at least, is still hot, and it's good.
Under the Count someone has chalked a small line in the corner: eleven years. Someone else has rubbed out the eleven and written ten.
A tired Gate officer takes the herbs you brought as a host gift, holds them up to the lamp and smells them before she scans them. 'Habit,' she says. 'The machine can't smell.'

Every evening the station ring is lit for an occasion, whether or not there is one. Tonight it's amber along the platform edge and a cool blue up by the cab core, and a little screen credits {painter}.
Off the car, an old woman who hasn't glided in years sits down on the nearest bench and laughs. Her granddaughter fetches her a broth and pretends not to be proud.
Glue and planed pear wood: the Quaysides here smell of the workshops, which start where the market stops. An apprentice carries a chair through the crowd upside down on her head.

Two families meet by accident at the ring counter: one gliding in to live here, one gliding out to live where the first came from. They arranged the swap over a month of messages, and shake hands now like old neighbours, which in a way they are.

Behind you the glide train backs into the jacket, and for a moment you can see the short dark tunnel it came through, fifty metres of it, with liquid hydrogen all round. Then the door slides shut and it's just a wall with a timetable on it.
Somebody's grandmother is holding up a sign that says {name}, and when you stop to read it she hugs you on the spot. She's never met her granddaughter's new partner and isn't taking chances.
Half the evening train is carrying dinner home from a neighbour's market: lidded pots, bread in cloth, a whole cheese in a net. The platform smells like everyone's kitchen at once.
Under the Ledger a volunteer with a box of keys looks up from a book. 'Three nights,' she says, 'and the hall's on {street},' and she draws the way on the back of your hand.
The counter cook catches you tasting and says it's {drum}'s broth, the best anywhere, and that the counter at {nb} puts sugar in theirs. You haven't asked. You gather that you will be asked, later.

You hear the hall before you see the Ledger: plates, a fiddle, a laugh that starts at one end of a long table and runs to the other. Somebody comes out to see who's arrived and goes back in to report.
Hot buns, from a basket under a cloth older than the man selling them: you buy one for a tenth of a kay and eat it standing up, which is how the platform eats everything.

Platform lamps are turned low here, to save light for the decks above, and the crowd moves through the half-dark from long practice. A girl of about ten takes your bag without asking, leads you to the cab queue, hands it back and runs.
After the catch your stomach takes a moment to agree with the rest of you. The counter cook has seen that face a thousand times and hands you the broth before you ask.
The commuter who sat beside you for a hundred and forty seconds says goodnight as if you'd known each other for years. Then she steps into a cab and goes up into the drum.
Past midnight a lone cleaner is mopping the platform in long, slow strokes, and you walk round the wet patch the way you'd walk round someone asleep.
Last train of the night. The counter's hatch is down, but there's an urn beside it, still warm, with a stack of cups and a sign: help yourself, wash your cup.
A couple are saying goodbye at the car door, one going back and one staying, in the practised way of people who glide to each other every week. They've done it so often they finish on the door chime.
One woman from your car stays a long time in front of the Ledger, reading the deaths. When she finds the name she touches it, says something you don't catch, and goes up.
At night the platform is lit no brighter than a reading lamp, and even the broth urn wears a felt cosy so its lid won't rattle. You drink in a silence that feels like being trusted with something.
A late freight crew moves crates of {nb}'s strawberries on quiet trolleys, talking under their breath so as not to wake anyone, though the nearest bedroom is fifteen decks up.
Off the car with you come two nurses going on shift and a cheerful man from a drum that sells its gin cheap, carrying two bottles of it as presents and very pleased to see the platform.
The Count glows over an empty platform. A woman off a night shift stops under it and reads both lines twice, the way people here do, as if the numbers might have moved while she was at work.
Asleep on the bench under the board is a man with his shoes off, and a capsule booking for the morning's first slow line tucked into one of them.
Dinner's long over at the station hall, but nobody has left. A dozen people are still at the long table, arguing gently, and one of them gets up to find you a bowl of whatever's left of the stew.
For a minute after the catch the platform sways, the way a floor sways after a long swim. It isn't moving. Your inner ear just hasn't been told.

Tomorrow's Hollow turns are posted by the cab core, deck by deck, with the elders' dawn hours at the top. An old man off the last train reads it with the quiet pleasure of someone who has finally got old enough.
Lamp-night in the drum above, but the Keel keeps working. Somewhere behind the wall the Vats' pumps go on slowly and evenly, like someone breathing in the next room.
The guest desk is shut, so you sign the night book on a stand under the Ledger, in a column of names going back a week. The guest above you has written {far}, a date and 'broth: excellent'.
Even at one in the morning the platform here is lit as if someone might be watching. The light is a low gold now, and it brightens a little ahead of you as you walk and dims again behind.
In a drum this full, night is just another shift. At one in the morning the platform is as busy as other drums' at six, and the cab queue is long, cheerful and in no hurry.
You're the only one off the car. The counter cook, who was reading, stands up anyway, warms a cup for you and goes back to the same page.
The crock room by the platform is lit all night: rows of starters working quietly under cloths, and a woman going down the rows with a spoon and a notebook, tasting.
Someone has left a bag of rice balls on the bench with a note: for whoever's off the last train. There are three left. You take one and leave the note.
Last off the car is a choir of eleven, still in their good clothes from a wedding one glide over. They sing one more verse on the platform, for nobody, before the cab takes them up.
Lamp-night at the Gate: one officer, a sequencer ticking in its bay, and an old woman from {nb} with a jar of yogurt she's kept alive for forty years. The officer is being very gentle with her.
Getting off a glide at this hour is like letting yourself into a house where everyone's asleep. You lower your voice, though there's nobody to hear it, and the heliox carries it anyway.
The first name on the Ledger today is a child born at twelve minutes past midnight, set beside a woman who died at a hundred and one. Two lines, and a share passed on.
Empty, clean and smelling of the night's cleaning fluid, the cab up leans into its climb, and by the time the doors open you've left a good part of your weight at the bottom.

A boy of about nine is waiting up on the platform for his mother's last train, wrapped in a blanket and very awake. When the doors open and she isn't on it, he says 'next one' to nobody and settles back down.

glide: The cradle lets go, and in about a second the weight goes out of everyone. A man across the aisle who has glided to work every day for thirty years still says "oh".
A bubble trapped in the window's metre of water stops climbing at the release and hangs perfectly still for the whole glide. At the catch it remembers which way is up.

For the first few seconds after the lamps dim, the window is black. Then your eyes catch up, and the rings of quay lights come out of the dark one rank at a time, all the way back to the vanishing point.

A girl has twisted round in her harness to press her face to the glass. Her father has told her, accurately, that the hall outside would kill her in minutes, and she wants to know if they can go slower.
{drum}, the drum you've just left, shrinks in the window: a bracelet of quay lights, then a ring for a finger, then one bright stitch among thousands.
Glide cars don't take hot soup, so the last thing everyone did on the platform was drink a whole cup of ring counter broth in four swallows. Half the car is still breathing through its mouth.
A young man who said goodbye to someone on the platform finds out that tears don't fall in a glide. They pool over one eye in a trembling lens until he takes them with his sleeve.
The commuters are asleep before the release and stay asleep through it, their arms floating up off the armrests as though every one of them had a question.

An old woman holds both armrests with her eyes shut for the whole hundred and forty seconds, and opens them only when the weight is back. "A young people's ride," she tells nobody in particular. Her great-grandson is a week old, and worth it.
Four lamp-painters are gliding over to {nb} to see a rival's dusk, and spend the whole way across agreeing that they're only going for the broth.
On the next lane level, a few hundred metres aft, a train let go at the same moment falls alongside yours, so its lit windows hang perfectly still in the dark, like a room you could step across into.

Mass costs nothing on the Glide, so the family moving to {nb} has brought everything: two children, four bags, a grandmother's table in the freight car, and a herb shelf in a crate marked for the Gate.
Around the seventieth second, the drum behind and the drum ahead are exactly the same size. Children who know about it go quiet for it.
The cradle takes the car on its soft arm, and over a second or two your weight comes back from wherever it went. Somebody says "oof" on behalf of everyone.
A man carries a starter crock in both arms the whole way, though nothing can fall in a glide, and keeps his thumb on the lid. At the catch he feels the starter settle inside it and breathes out.
Out here it is never night. The rings of quay lights shine the same at one in the morning as at noon, because there is nothing outside for a clock to mean.
The Gate's night crew from Ring {ring} are going home together and are all asleep before the release. One of them still has a sample label stuck to her cuff.

A couple sits with a padded bag strapped into the seat between them: a remade chair, older than both of them together, going to a wedding in {nb}. Each of them keeps a hand on it, though it isn't going anywhere.
Everyone in the wedding party carries two bottles of gin, the most the drum ahead lets in without duty, and every bag clinks once at the release and once at the catch.
For a hundred and forty seconds the train falls in a perfectly straight line at 174 metres a second, and all of it feels like sitting very still in a room that has forgotten which way is down.
The release lifts every loose hair in the car at once, and for two minutes everyone looks as though they've put their heads under at the baths.
A boy counts down to the release out loud and gets it wrong by a second. The weight goes on "one" instead of "nought", and he shouts anyway.
About a minute in, it occurs to you that the small ring of lights in the window has two hundred million people inside it, and that you slept in one of their flats last night.

Most of the window is dark: a hall nearly four kilometres deep, with the radiator layer running away overhead like the ceiling of the world. The drums go up into it like pillars, and you can only tell where they are by their lights.

An aunt explains to a small boy that nobody pays for a glide, because one drum throws you and the next one catches you. He thinks about it all the way across, and at the catch he says "thank you" to the wall.
A single lit cradle slides round the waist of the drum ahead, riding the quay band to meet somebody else's train. It's the only thing in the window that shows the drum is turning at all.
The car dims its lamps after the release so the window isn't just a picture of your own face. In the dark, everyone's voice drops too.
Along the bottom of the inner pane, at exactly the height of a six-year-old, runs a band of small handprints that the cleaners never quite get to.
Eighty crates of tomatoes ride in the freight car, sealed and certified, and their trader spends the glide reading the certificates again, as if one of them might have changed its mind.
Far out in the dark, a train on a crossing lane slips across behind yours, a short string of lit windows, and is gone before anyone can point.

The Glide needs no power, so it ran all through the Eleven Days, with drums along every row passing food and parts to each other in cars like this one. An old man in the front row lays his palm flat on the wall at the release, as if greeting someone.
Your stomach lifts at the release as though the car had gone over a bump, and then simply stays lifted.
In the last twenty seconds the drum ahead stops being a ring of lights and becomes a wall: dark, curved and far too big, filling the window from edge to edge.
Two students throw a pen back and forth across the aisle. In here it flies in a perfectly straight line, which nothing thrown inside a drum ever does, and they can't get over it.
A woman coming home from a funeral in {nb} holds a remade coat folded on her lap and doesn't look at the window once.
The catch is a long, soft lean into your seat: a second or two of weight pouring back in, until you weigh exactly what you weighed on the platform.
A boy with his hair combed flat for someone in {nb} carries a single sprig of basil in a twist of paper. He checks it at the release, at the halfway point and at the catch.

Nearest, the drums are dark pillars six kilometres across. Farther off they're only their rings of light, and farther still the rings run together at a vanishing point you could cover with a fingernail.
On her father's lap, sharing his harness, a small girl spends the glide trying to drop her shoe. It won't go.
A drop of water gets loose from someone's flask at the release and wobbles across the aisle as a perfect bead. Four people watch it, and nobody wants to be the one who catches it.
The nearest quay lights slide past, the far ones hardly move, and the ones at the vanishing point don't move at all, so the whole hall seems to turn slowly on a pin a long way off.
A girl with a black thread round her left wrist spends the glide reading nothing and answering nothing, only looking, and decides it's the best two minutes of her day.
"Is this outside?" a small boy asks. "This is outside," his mother says, and they both look at it as if it might hear them.
Near the end, the cradle waiting at the touch point is the brightest thing in the window, sliding round the drum's waist at exactly your speed. For the last few seconds it seems not to move at all.
When the catch is done your bag has its weight back, and a bit more, because the rim of a drum is a full g and nobody lives that heavy.
Someone has fallen asleep with their cheek against the window, a metre of water between their face and a hall that would kill them in minutes. Nobody wakes them. There are worse pillows.
Between two distant drums a thread of lights crawls across the dark: a train on another lane, so far away that 174 metres a second looks like walking pace.
From the platform a glide car looks like a squat block of sealed water with a door in it, which is very nearly what it is. The water keeps the hall's X-rays out, and the same water makes the window.
Three teenagers at the back have agreed not to hold on to anything for the whole glide. At the catch they all grab the same armrest.
An old man glided to work every day for fifty years and never once looked out. Now that he has stopped working, he rides over and back once a week just to look.
A flute case 1.2 metres long lies across three laps, and its owner apologises to all three at the release, when it floats gently up off them and has to be held down.
At the release a small sound runs the length of the train: two hundred people taking the same breath at once.
Every one of those rings has two hundred million people inside it, and somewhere out in the dark a train full of them is gliding too, looking at yours.
The release catches a man halfway through a pastry, and the crumbs lift off his shirt and hang round his head until the catch puts every one of them back in his lap.
Two neighbours who have commuted together for eleven years have never once spoken during a glide. It's the only quiet place either of them knows.
The {block} choir is gliding to a wedding and has been asked not to sing in the car. They hum instead, all forty of them, which in heliox is very nearly singing.
A girl in the front row tries to count the rings of quay lights before the catch. She gets to forty-one, loses her place behind a crossing train, and starts again.
When the weight goes, the tray of lidded dumplings on a man's knees floats up a finger's width, and he keeps it there with one flat hand, like someone calming a friend.
The car makes almost no sound in the glide. Nothing is pushing it and nothing is pushing back, and you can hear someone three seats away breathing.

The last glide back to {drum} is at one in the morning and full of people from weddings: loosened collars, cake wrapped in napkins, a child asleep across two seats and floating gently against the harness.
A courier for the strain library has a case of sealed cultures on her knees, and at the catch she murmurs "there we are" to it, the way you'd settle a baby.
A man moving drums alone has one bag and a pot of chives. At the halfway point he holds the chives up to the window, so they can see.
At the catch every loose thing in the car comes down at once, with a soft general patter: pens, crumbs, a hair clip, somebody's sock.
A metre of water makes a very good window. The only sign it's there at all is a faint blue-green at the edges, where you look through it at a slant.
A grandmother has brought her grandson on his first glide, and spends the whole of it watching his face instead of the window.
The rule on the platform is that anything loose goes in a pocket. The rule is for other people, which is why a comb is drifting down the aisle.
On the first train of the working day nobody looks out at all. A hall that would kill them in minutes, lit by the rings of a thousand drums, is to them the bit between breakfast and the Vats.
Across the aisle, a wanderer on the first glide of her year watches her home drum shrink until it's one ring among thousands, and then, she admits to you, she loses track of which.

Every {weekday} for {years} years, two old friends a glide apart have taken turns making the trip. The one beside you is carrying a jar of pickles and a grievance from last week, and is looking forward to both.

Once in a long while a cradle lets a car go by, and the lane simply carries it on to the next drum in the row, a hundred and forty seconds further. Today it happens to your train, and the younger half of the car cheers.
cycler: The capsule runs up its ramp, and for three and a half minutes a full g presses you back into the couch. Then a clunk, a hiss, a green light, and the hatch opens onto a train that hasn't stopped since before you were born.
You find out how weightless the slow line is the moment the hatch opens: your bag goes in ahead of you and keeps going.

The train neither slows nor waits at a station. Capsules come up their ramps, match it, dock and open, and anyone getting off has to be strapped in and ready at their minute or ride on to the next station, a day or more away.

Somebody always sleeps through their capsule. This leg it's {name}, who was meant to get off at the last station and is now, quite cheerfully, going two days further to drums nobody aboard has heard of.

Leaving is quick. The capsule undocks, the train goes on without you at two kilometres a second, and the ramp brakes you for three and a half minutes into a drum's tube, where the weight comes back before your legs are ready.
After nine days weightless, the first hour back in a drum is comic. Your bag seems to have been packed with someone else's things, and every stair is a conversation with your knees.
When riders leave, the Galley sends each of them off with a bulb of stock from the pot, to drink on their first platform beside a ring counter that is serving a different broth and losing.
Every new rider comes through the hatch carrying the smell of a drum: a hall's stew, a flat's laundry soap, the cut grass of somebody's Hollow.
The Wanderers' Galley stockpot is a sealed crock with a crank on the side, and it hasn't gone cold in living memory. Whoever floats past gives the crank a turn without being asked.

Every rider adds something from the last drum they slept in. Today the pot has had a sprig of shiso, a rind of vat cheese, a spoon of somebody's mother's miso, and a heel of bread from a hall nobody else has heard of.

The Galley log lists what went into the pot and who put it there, in a hundred hands going back past the oldest writing anyone aboard can read. You add your line: three basil leaves, from a guest flat's herb shelf in {drum}.
Two riders from neighbouring drums have been arguing about broth since the second day. The Galley has started taking sides, and someone is keeping score on the wall.
Nobody aboard can say for certain whether the stockpot is good. It tastes of more drums than anyone has counted, and every rider swears it tastes different the day after they add to it.
Stock from the pot comes out in bulbs, and the rule is to squeeze slowly. Squeeze fast and a ball of hot broth wobbles off across the Galley, with three people after it holding cups.
There's no cook on the slow line. The Galley belongs to whoever rides, and the rota on the wall is in eleven different hands, one of them yours.
At the evening turn of the crank, the longest-serving rider reads out what went into the pot that day. It takes a while, and nobody hurries it.
Someone adds a spoon of the Nine to the stockpot, and there is a short, serious debate about whether that counts as something from a drum.
A rider from a wood drum adds one dried mushroom to the pot and writes nothing in the log. Three days later she says her first word aboard, which is "salt".
The Galley costs about half a kay a day beyond the commons. A sign over the pot calls it the best half-kay on the raft, and the sign has been repainted more often than the Galley has.

The crock shelf runs the length of the Galley, and the oldest crocks have been relabelled so many times that the labels are mostly ink. Take a spoon, leave a spoon: nobody has ever seen the rule written down.
You take a spoon of rye starter labelled "{far}, very sour, sorry" and leave a spoon of yours, labelled rather more confidently than it deserves.
A starter at zero g doesn't rise; it swells, every way at once, into a pale soft ball that has to be coaxed back into its crock.
One crock on the shelf is marked "for Spelt" in big letters: spoons for the baker who makes the raft loaf, carried along the line by whoever's going that way.
At the next stop the Gate will sequence everything in your crock before it lets it in. Tonight, in the Galley, it's just bread, and everyone wants to smell it.
Somebody's yogurt culture has been on the crock shelf so long that it has its own line in the log and its own birthday, which the Galley keeps with a spoon each.
A woman of seventy is riding the slow line again, fifty years after her wander year, and has found her own line in the Galley log: her own handwriting, a little bolder.
Soup comes in bulbs, bread in a net, and jam in a tube you squeeze onto the bread one careful stripe at a time, because anything spread too thick leaves.
Somebody tries to pull noodles in the Galley. Without weight a strand doesn't stretch, it wanders, and the rest of the evening goes on catching ribbons of dough out of the air with chopsticks.
Every dish aboard is lidded, not for manners but because otherwise it leaves. For once nobody can tell anything about your upbringing.

For the first few days your taste goes flat, because without weight your face fills up as if you had a cold. The Galley keeps three tins of the Nine and a jar of chilli crisp by the pot, and they go fast.
Crumbs are the enemy. They don't fall, they spread, and the train's air filters are lined with a fine grey flour of every loaf on the raft.
Drinking from a bulb takes a day to learn. Squeeze too hard and a ball of tea floats past your nose, hot, shining and entirely your problem.
Mill jook comes in a squeeze pouch and tastes, everyone agrees, exactly like Mill jook in a bowl, which is the most comforting thing about it.
A rider has brought one tomato from the {row} drums and cuts it into seven pieces inside a sealed bag, so the juice can't get away. Seven people eat their piece very slowly.
Every evening there's an argument about whether a bulb of Mill lager can be called a pint. The lager is free and bulbs are all there is, so the argument is mostly about dignity.
Dinner is eaten in a loose ring round the stockpot with nobody quite the right way up, and a newcomer's first lesson is that you can't put a bulb down, only let go of it.

A rider teaches the Galley her table's dumpling fold. At zero g the filling won't sit in the wrapper and has to be caught there, and by the end there's filling on the ceiling, which is also the floor.
Somebody opens a side salad in the Galley as carefully as a letter. Every leaf goes into a mouth before it can go anywhere else.
Sleeping bags clip to the wall like coats on hooks, and you sleep upright, or sideways, or any way you like, since none of them is up.
A small fan by every bunk keeps the air moving, because without weight warm breath doesn't rise. Switch it off and you wake an hour later with a headache, inside a pocket of your own breathing.
Without weight your arms drift up while you sleep. Most riders learn to tuck their hands into the bag's straps after one morning of waking nose to knuckle with themselves.
The train keeps a lamp clock of its own: up at half past six, down at eleven. Riders from drums that run late grumble about it for a week and then forget they ever lived any other way.
At night the sleeping car is forty bags along two walls, the fans, the soft click of the train's pumps, and someone muttering in their sleep in an accent from the far side.
The first night aboard you dream of stairs. Everyone does, the riders say, and by the fourth night you won't dream of anything at all.
Your sleeping bag has had a great many owners, and each has mended it somewhere. The newest patch is a square of hard algae blue, and there's room for yours.
One rider sleeps in the Galley with a hand hooked through the crock shelf's rail, because it's the warmest place on the train and it smells of bread.
At three in the morning by the train's clock, the only lights are the board and the stockpot's little lamp, and somebody is always awake, floating by the pot, writing.
The bungee hour is every day, an hour on straps and cords that pull you toward a floor that isn't there, "or your bones sulk". Riders say it the way people at home say "have some Nine".
By the third day your face has gone round and your legs have gone thin, as the blood forgets which way is down. Everyone looks a little younger and a little sillier.
Whoever has been aboard longest leads the bungee hour, and on this train that's a quiet man of forty-four going home to {far} from a job. He counts in a whisper, and nobody skips.
You grow about two centimetres on a slow line, as your spine stops being squeezed, and lose them again on your first day back in a drum.
