Moving well at zero g is a matter of fingertips. By the fourth day you cross the Galley with one push and arrive exactly where you meant to, and you're prouder of it than of anything else this year.
Newcomers fling themselves down the car and hit every wall. Old hands move with two fingers on the rail, like someone following a line in a book.
Shoes are no use aboard. Everyone goes in grip socks, and by the second week the sleeping car smells faintly of everyone's feet, which nobody mentions.
Most riders are twenty and on their wander year, so anyone past twenty-five is "aunt". Past thirty it's "big aunt", and everyone assumes you know where the spare bulbs are kept.
Riders trade drums like recipes: where the guest flats keep the best herb shelves, which hall lets you stay on if you cook, which ring counter has a broth worth getting off for.
A rider from the {farrow} drums says "kays" like "keys", and the whole Galley has opinions about it.
Someone has started a wall of notes by the capsule bay, one per drum: "Bring a slate." "Learn crosswise." "The aunt at Ring 4 is lying about the pears."

{name} and {name2} met on the second day, both reaching for the last net of bread, and have eaten every meal together since. The rest of the Galley has begun to suspect they'll get off at the same station.
Every rider's first question to every other rider is "Where did you sleep last?" The second is "What did they feed you?"
A rider from a counted drum answers questions about the fitting for ten minutes, because people ask kindly, and then asks for the chilli crisp, because that's enough of that.
There's always one rider who has done the whole raft and wants you to know it. On this train it's a woman of twenty-three with a crosswise flyer's shoulders and a story for every row.
A rider from a hall drum has never eaten alone and isn't going to start now. By the second day she has the Galley laying a table, which at zero g means a long strap everyone hooks a foot under.
Two riders going home to the same drum after a year away have been rehearsing what they'll say at the station ring for six days. Neither has said the same thing twice.
An old couple rides the slow line every few years on their anniversary, in the same two berths, and the Galley makes them a cake that won't stay on its plate.

A family is moving across the raft to be near a grandmother. By the second day their three-year-old swims through the air better than anyone aboard, and has to be told that the new flat will have a floor.
Someone plays a heliox flute in the sleeping car after the lamps go down, very softly, and nobody asks them to stop, which on a slow line is the highest praise there is.
A choir forms by the fourth day, as it always seems to. By the second week it has songs from eleven drums and a feud about the alto line.
A rider teaches the Galley a reel from a third-g terrace. At zero g it turns into something nobody has a name for, with everyone slowly turning over and nobody able to stop.
Riders write the drums they've slept in on the inside flap of the sleeping bag. One bag has two hundred and six names in it, the oldest so faded they have to be read with a lamp held sideways.
A big aunt of thirty-four has been asked to settle six arguments today: two about broth, one about who kissed whom first, and three about whose turn it is at the crank.
Riders ask each other where they're from by row, not drum, because nobody has ever heard of anybody's drum.
A rider's grandmother has sent a long letter aboard, and with her permission it's read out in the Galley. Half the Galley ends up writing back to a woman they'll never meet.
A rider going to {far} to marry has nothing to say about the drum and everything to say about the person waiting there.
Riders play slow worlds in the Galley, games built to tolerate minutes of lag, against people a metre away. It feels so wrong that they add a delay back in.
Every day the light home gets about half a second longer. You notice it first as a pause before every answer that wasn't there last week, and then you notice yourself writing longer.
There's a desk in the Galley for long letters, with a lamp, a strap for your feet and a slate, and a queue for it every evening. A long letter is written carefully, to be read once.
You tell home a joke and wait. On the first day it landed in a couple of seconds; now it takes ten, and you've learned to tell the joke and then go and turn the crank.
Black threads are common on slow lines: no worlds, no messages, and nine and a half kays a day going into the travel account instead. The dark riders talk to each other more than anyone on the train.
A card home is written in the Galley, postmarked with the day and the light delay, and sent the instant you finish. The postmark is the part home reads first.
A rider eleven months out writes to her mother with thirty seconds of light each way, and has learned to write in paragraphs, like someone writing to the past.
News of a birth at home reaches a rider eight seconds after it was sent, and the Galley opens a bulb of wine to drink to a child a day old and two and a half million kilometres away.
A rider gets bad news from home the same way as good: a few seconds late, in a voice that has already finished crying. Nobody says much. Somebody turns the crank for her.
Two riders who met in a slow world years ago, across forty seconds of light, have met in person on this train. For the first hour they keep pausing before they answer each other.
A rider writes the same long letter four times and sends none of them. On the fifth day she sends a card that says only "Fed, fine, thinking of you".
Messages from home arrive with the delay printed in the corner. Every morning the number is a little bigger, and every morning someone in the Galley reads theirs out like a temperature.
A rider sends a song to her grandmother, and twenty seconds later a reply begins: her grandmother singing the second verse, a little flat, from three million kilometres away.
There are no windows. The trunk is a shielded tube, and the only view of outside is a board in the Galley showing the rows go by.
Two kilometres a second is a drum every twelve seconds, about seven thousand a day, and you can't see a single one of them. The board counts them anyway, and somebody reads the total out at dinner.
When the board ticks over to a row someone aboard was born on, the Galley gives a small cheer, and the rider tells everyone what the ring counter broth is like there.
The board says you passed {far} at twelve minutes past two this afternoon: two hundred million people, a dozen kilometres away through the tube wall. You were asleep.
On the board's map of Merrow a whole week of travel moves your little light about a hand's width. Riders measure what's left of the leg in fingers.
In the second week the rows on the board stop being names you know. Then they stop being names anyone aboard knows, and the Galley gets very interested in whoever comes through the hatch next.
Some rows on the board have names, like Herb and Bell and Kelp. Most are only pairs of numbers, stretches of drums too ordinary for anyone to have named them together.
Washing aboard is a wet flannel, a squeeze of no-rinse soap and a towel held ready, in a curtained stall with your feet under a strap. Somebody always sings in there, because the stall rings.

Haircuts happen in the Galley with a vacuum hose held by the scissors, so every snipped end goes straight down it. The best cutter aboard is {name}, nineteen, who charges nothing but likes to be told it's good.
The air return grille at the end of the sleeping car is the train's lost property office. This week it has given back two spoons, an earring, a black thread, and a letter nobody will admit to.
A cleaning robot the size of a loaf works its way along the Galley walls after every meal, hunting crumbs. Every leg the riders give it a new name, and it answers to none of them.
The toilet door has a diagram with nine numbered steps, and generations of riders have added a tenth in pencil, each one different.

Laundry is a sealed bag, a squirt of soapy water and ten minutes of kneading, then a day clipped to a line in front of the fans, where every shirt stands straight out like a crowd trying to leave by the same door.
Spilled water doesn't run anywhere. It clings to the wall in a trembling blister until somebody comes with a towel, and on a slow line somebody always does.
A hair clip floated off on the first day, and the whole train has been passing it hand to hand for a week, looking for its owner.
The Quiet in a tube is very quiet. No worlds, no messages, nothing on the board but the rows, and forty riders round the stockpot, talking until the lamps go down.

Booking Day arrives as one line on the board: the beam for the year, flat, as it nearly always is. The riders pool what the Quiet saved them, and somebody has an orchard apple, cut crosswise so the whole Galley can see the star.
On Booking night the riders hold their own Long Flight, forty metres of it, from one end of the sleeping car to the other with hand lamps. Nobody needs wing-sleeves.
Knotnight aboard is a short evening: lamps down, every rider's leftovers on the table, and a larder made out of them, knotted into a net and hung by the pot for whoever is hungry next week.
A rider spends Knotnight showing the Galley how her block ties the knots on its larder bags, and by the end of the evening every crock on the shelf is wearing one.

A rider is going home to {far} for Homecoming and has been counting it down on the board for ten days. The Galley makes her a hand lamp out of a bulb and a strip light, so she'll have one to hold up when she sees theirs.
The slow line costs 1.1 kays whatever the distance, about a fifth of a new shirt. You're buying time, not distance, and the slow line has more of it to sell than anyone.
Riders mend aboard, because there's time. The Galley keeps a basket of offcuts, and by the end of the line half the coats on the train have a patch from a drum their owners never slept in.
A rider has brought her herb shelf: one pot of basil in a clear bag, roots going every way at once, under a lamp clipped to her berth. It's the most visited thing on the train.
Two stewards live aboard for half the year at a time and know the stockpot better than anyone. By old custom they never add to it, only taste.
A man going to a job on the far side, not a wanderer at all, has started teaching the twenty-year-olds to make jook properly, and now they won't let him go to bed.
Slow riders are mostly young because the slow line costs time, and the young have the most of it. The old ones aboard are the ones who've decided they do too.
A rider has been aboard forty days without getting off, which is allowed and unusual, and the Galley has begun to treat her as part of the train, asking her where things are kept.
Riders name their berths for the length of a leg. Berth {n} on this train is called "the cupboard", for reasons its current owner won't explain.
There's a rule that whoever spills the stockpot cleans the air filters. Nobody has spilled it in living memory, which the riders find suspicious.
Halfway along the leg the Galley holds a swap. New things are dear and riders travel light, so it's mostly socks, songs and spoons of starter.
The train has a little clinic and a nurse who rides half the year. Most of what she treats is homesickness, and she treats it with a bulb from the pot.
Weekdays slide aboard. Riders find out it's {weekday} from home, a few seconds late, and are always faintly surprised.

Express: Thirty-four minutes up the ramp at a full g, lying back with the capsule's tail for a floor, until you're doing twenty kilometres a second and the capsule docks. Then nothing weighs anything for about thirteen hours.
Express: 111 kays, about five days of a wallet, for a million kilometres in about sixteen hours. Nobody aboard is wandering; everyone is going to something.

Express: The car is very quiet. Across the aisle a man is going to a birth, two seats down a woman is going to a funeral, and the girl by the board is going to someone in {far} she has only ever spoken to with a seven-second wait.

Express: At the far end the couches turn round to face the way you came, so the braking ramp presses you into them instead of out. Thirty-four minutes later you're in a drum the slow line would have taken six days to reach.

Express: Merrow has run its trunks fast since the Eleven Days, so that braking the trains could keep the air going for months. "You're riding on the Eleven Days," an old man tells the boy beside him, who is going to his first job and nods politely.

Express: At the station you stand by the express ramp for a long time, doing the sum: five days of wallet, there by {weekday}. Then you go and find the slow capsule, because the slow line has a stockpot and the express only has a counter.
Express: Dinner is quiet and dear and nobody minds. The galley here is a counter with a cook, and the soup was made this morning, which slow riders would find faintly shocking.

Express: A young woman has been dark for twelve days to pay for this seat and still wears the black thread. She takes it off at the dock, switches her worlds back on, and watches the wait for each reply get shorter by the hour.
Express: The light delay to his mother's drum shrinks on the board by a quarter of a second an hour, and the man going to her bedside watches nothing else for sixteen hours.
Express: Slow riders laugh at the express for being over before you've learned anyone's name. Nobody on the express is there to learn anyone's name.

hollow.t: The cab pavilion opens onto lawns still grey from the lamp-night. Overhead the far bank is dark but for its path lamps, and the sunline is only a warm brown thread.
Nothing casts a long shadow at dawn here. The light comes from straight overhead all day long; dawn only turns it up, warm and then white.
{painter}'s dawn starts in the brown-violet the back crews call bruise and takes an hour to decide on gold. Nobody on the terraces says a word until it does.
Lamp-dawn at the lake belongs to the elders. Forty of them swim slow lengths side by side, heads up, talking the whole way, and one waves you in and promises that only the first length is cold.

At the orchard gate a class of six-year-olds waits with brushes on sticks. It's the blossom weeks, and someone has to carry the pollen from flower to flower, so they do, one blossom at a time, very seriously.

Early in the dawn you can still look straight at the sunline: a warm thread running almost from end wall to end wall, a kilometre and a half up. By eight it's too bright, and you wish you'd looked longer.
Overhead, the far bank's cab pavilions open one by one, small lit doors three kilometres up. The first people of the day step out of them upside down and set off along the paths.
Six elders, two swimmers and a baker with a tray of buns for the lake bench ride the first cab up. The baker calls it a standing arrangement that nobody remembers starting.
Today's dawn is unpainted, a plain ramp, warm and then white. People still stop on the paths to watch it, the way people at home look up when the lamps come on.
In the bamboo grove the dawn comes through in green stripes. It's quiet enough that you can hear someone a hundred metres off unwrapping breakfast.
A woodwarden passes you on the path and holds up a slate that already says GOOD MORNING, as though it had been waiting all night for someone to show it to.
On the top terrace a girl jumps for a pear on the wall, rises past it to the height of a house, and lands several metres spinward of where she took off, which seems to be the point.

Gardeners water the top terraces at lamp-dawn, and up there the spray from a hose climbs in a slow arc, hangs, and comes down somewhere other than the bed it was aimed at. The gardeners aim accordingly.
Near the end walls the floor stays dim long after mid-floor is bright, because the sunline stops short of them. Old people carry their tea down there for a slower morning.

Someone left a hand lamp on the grass last night, still glowing, a watt of white beside the path. A child picks it up, looks round for its owner, and carries it solemnly to the lost-things box at the pavilion.

The swell paddles start at the end of the dawn. The first waves come across the lake slow and tall, five seconds apart, and the elders who've had the water since six climb out like people whose house has filled with guests.
A board at the cab pavilion lists today's turns deck by deck, and at the bottom, in a different hand: GUESTS, ONE HOUR, WELCOME. Someone has underlined WELCOME twice.
At lamp-dawn the lake is flat, and the far bank lies in it, upside down twice over, which puts it the right way up.
Dawn is the cheap hour in a drum that sells its Hollow time, and the meadow is full of people who decided they could do without sleep. Most of them are asleep on the grass.
{painter} is in the coffee queue on the back terraces, cup in hand, pretending not to listen. Ask whose dawn it is and the whole queue turns round.
This painter starts the dawn at the far end of the line and lets it travel toward you, so the light arrives the way someone comes up a long hall carrying a lamp.
A runner lopes past on the lake path, a few metres to a stride, wearing the fixed smile of someone who has just found out how far half a g lets a person go.
Before the crowds come up you can hear how big the Hollow is: a mower somewhere along the bank, a gate, a child calling a name, each sound bright and small and a long way from the next.
For twenty minutes the line runs rose, and the whole upside-down town on the far bank turns pink, pavilions and paths and people, as if it had been embarrassed into getting up.
An old woman on the elders' bench is knitting something long and algae-blue for a naming. She comes up every lamp-dawn, she says, because the light is good, the company is quiet, and both are free.

Pickers are up in the orchard on ladders that would be dangerous at the rim and are only interesting here. Each apple goes into a padded crate like a jewel, which at four and a half kays it nearly is.
Your hour starts at seven. The warden at the pavilion stamps a small green leaf on the back of your hand, which will fade in about an hour, and says that's how it has always been done.
A choir on the third terrace sings the line up, bright heliox voices thrown out across the floor, one held note for every change of colour.

A kite-maker sets out paper kites on a cloth by the pavilion, big and light and cut for half a g, and explains to a doubtful child that a kite here flies only while you run, so choose one worth running for.

In a thin drum, lamp-dawn is the Hollow's only quiet hour. By eight the turns begin and the lawns fill shoulder to shoulder, so people come at six and sit very still, as if quiet could be saved for later.
Somebody's grandmother is doing slow exercises on the lawn, and at half a g her raised leg takes its time coming down. She holds it up a moment longer than she needs to, out of pride.
The line runs gold at one end this morning and rose at the other: two painters sharing a dawn, and the place where their halves meet was argued over for a month.
Under the yews it's still dark at six, and a woodwarden is raking the path by feel, the rake's teeth ticking in the quiet.
At full noon you learn to look up at an angle. The line itself is a white bar too bright to bear, but on either side of it the far bank hangs in plain view, every path and pavilion sharp.

At noon your shadow is a small pool round your feet, sharp-edged spinward and antispinward and blurred toward the end walls, because the light comes from a line along the axis. Children here draw shadows that way.
On the next cloth a family has pastries, crackers, gin and soda, and a single tomato on a plate of its own, under its own lid, like a guest of honour.
Water at half a g is slow. A splash goes up, hangs, and comes down in fat drops, and the children in the shallows spend the whole hour making it do that again.
A boy on the high board works up his nerve for ten minutes, then drops, and at half a g he has time to change his mind twice on the way down.
On the far bank, three kilometres overhead, a child runs with a kite and the kite climbs toward you on its string. Nothing here blows; every kite in the Hollow is up because somebody is running.
Noon is too bright to read in. Half the meadow lies on its back with jackets over its face, like a field of sleeping coats.
Climbing the end wall's terraces, you lose a little weight at every tier. Halfway up your stride turns into a lope, and near the top the stairs are more of a suggestion.
An orchard warden on a ladder is tying paper bags over the best apples one by one, each bag pencilled with a family name and a wedding date.
This drum buys a longer noon than most, and its people use every minute: at six in the evening the lawns are still full, still squinting, still in their good clothes.
At swell hour the lake is full of people treading water, waiting for the fifth wave, which everyone agrees is the good one, though nobody can say why.
The lake at noon is mostly heads. The lifeguard's whistle, pitched up by the heliox, sounds as if it belongs to a much smaller lifeguard.
Two pavilions over, a wedding is cutting its apple. The officiant holds up the halves, a hundred guests lean in to see the star of seeds, and so do you, from a picnic cloth thirty metres away.
A slate hangs on a birch at the edge of the dim wood: TALK OUTSIDE. Inside, noon is a green half-light, and the only sound is the drum itself: fans, water, a pump somewhere far off.
A hammock slung between two pear trees barely sags under half a g. Its occupant is reading and refuses to look up at anything, including the far bank.
At noon the great square is the brightest place you've ever stood: pale tiles, lit fountains, a band in a pavilion, and a board showing how many kays of rent went back to every resident last month.
You spend your hour lying on your back on the grass, looking up at the far bank and the people on it, who are lying on their backs looking at you.
Bamboo makes the Hollow's only proper shade at noon, and the grove is full of elders on folding stools who got there first and mean to stay.
Half a g turns a game of catch into a conversation. The ball goes up, hangs, and comes down a little spinward of where anyone meant it to, and both players have time to remark on it.
The pavilion desk has a ticket waiting for you: one Hollow hour, paid for by {name}, whom you met at the hall last night and who never mentioned it.
Looking up feels less like looking up than looking across. The far bank is lit exactly as yours is, three kilometres off, as if the Hollow were a single room the size of a nation.
A man asleep on the grass with a jacket over his eyes is wearing a paper crown, and the children responsible are watching him from behind a pear tree with tremendous restraint.
Each guest may pick one pear from the orchard's low branches, one and only one. You take a long time choosing, and the warden, who has seen this before, waits.
From below you can watch a wedding reel on the third-g terrace. Every leap comes down a hand's width spinward, so the whole ring of dancers creeps slowly round the terrace as it goes.
At noon the paths are full enough to have a direction, like corridors at a shift change, and a warden at the big crossing keeps them moving with a flag on a pole.
The meadow by the lake is left long, with flowers in it that nobody has to eat, which in a drum this crowded is the height of luxury.
A girl on the far bank is waving at you, and has been for some time. When you finally wave back she jumps, comes down slowly, and runs off to tell someone.
Lamp-noon in a counted drum's Hollow: plenty of room on the grass and not many small children, and the few there are being watched by a great many adults.
In a thin drum the noon turn is twenty minutes long, and the lawn is so full that people sit back to back and take turns lying down.
A terrace stall sells cold tea and pastry for almost nothing and the view for nothing at all: the whole Hollow curling up and over, a lake on the ceiling, people walking about on it.
Somewhere on the lawn a heliox flute is being played badly by someone very happy. It carries a long way, which is the only problem.
Picnics come under lids, even on the grass. The family beside you forgets, and their grandmother covers the dish with her hat without looking up from her book.
Races on the lawn are always run anti. Spinward you get heavier with every stride and antispinward lighter, and at half a g that's the difference between trudging and flying.
Under full noon the floor is warm through your shoes and the air is warm on your face, and for an hour you forget that every other room you've ever been in had a ceiling three metres up.
Children from {block} are holding a jumping contest on the terraces, starting one tier higher each round, until the smallest wins by being nearly weightless.
Under the birches at the lake's end is the one place on the floor where leaves hide the far bank, and every couple in the drum seems to know it.
Dusk begins at three. The line eases from white to gold over the first hour, and the far bank comes back as something you can look at, full of people heading for the pavilions.
{painter}'s dusk goes down through amber into a long violet and holds the violet so long that people on the terraces start to laugh. Then it goes out, and they clap.
At the end of a turn the wardens walk the lawns ringing small bells. A whole deck folds its picnic cloths and heads for the pavilions, while the next deck comes up out of the ground behind it.
The far bank's path lamps come on overhead: a lit map of a town you could walk to in an hour, the long way round the floor, and probably never will.
As the gold fades the lifeguards draw in the swimming lines hand over hand, and the lake turns from a public place back into a private one, with only a few night swimmers' heads left in it.
Twenty-five minutes before lamp-night the middle of the Spindle opens, and the first flyers come out along the axis with their hand lamps, small and white against the dimming line.
In this drum the painters save their best for dusk. 'Anyone can paint a dawn,' says the woman beside you on the terrace. 'People are grateful for any light at all.'
A family packs its picnic away with great care, and the last thing into the basket is the tomato's own small plate, empty and wiped clean.
Dusk on the top terrace: light enough to sit on the rail and swing your feet, with the whole Hollow below and above you going gold and then grey.
A choir on the lowest terrace sings the line down. The last note lasts longer than the light does.
At dusk the woodwardens come out with slates: CLOSING SOON. A second line, smaller: PLEASE TAKE YOUR VOICES WITH YOU.
Someone starts a game of tag on the meadow as the light goes amber. Half a g turns it into a game of enormous leaps and shrieking, and the adults pretend they don't want to join.
In a thin drum the turn changes at the first gold, and a fresh crowd comes up out of the ground to sit where you were sitting, while the grass is still warm.
Overhead the far bank's lake holds the last gold, a long bright shape hanging upside down, and it goes grey at exactly the same moment as the lake at your feet.
A sign goes up at the orchard gate as the light goes amber: THE PEARS HAVE BEEN COUNTED. It is meant kindly, mostly.
Seats on the end-wall terraces go by auction for a painted dusk, and the rents go back to everyone in the drum, so the people who lost the bidding go home slightly richer than the people who won.
Couples walk the lake path slowly in the long dusk. Even slowly has a little float in it here.
A kite comes down on your bank with its string trailing. The child chasing it arrives a minute later, out of breath, and asks you to hold it while the tail gets fixed.
With the dusk the swell paddles stop, and the last waves come in slower and smaller until the lake lies flat and starts to hold the path lamps.
Under the gold, an old man on the elders' bench tells you he has watched most of the dusks of the last sixty years from that bench. This one, he says, was ordinary, and he seems pleased about it.
In the bamboo the path lamps come on low and white, and the culms lay still stripes across them. Somebody's grandfather is asleep on a bench in one of the bright bits.
In the last red minutes of dusk the far bank turns the colour of the inside of a closed eyelid, and the small boy beside you shuts his eyes to check.
The last guests of the day queue at the pavilion for the cabs down, and it's the friendliest queue in the drum, because everyone in it has just spent an hour with room to see.
A painter's assistant on the terrace below calls timings into a handset, 'amber for forty, rose, hold, hold', and the dusk overhead does exactly as it's told.
Children are called home off the lawns as the gold goes, name by name, and in heliox the names carry right across the floor, so half the Hollow learns who's late for dinner.
The guests' turn here is the late one, nine to eleven, when the lawns belong to people who work days and the talk on the benches is mostly about rotas.
Once the line goes dark the Hollow cools by a few degrees, a jacket's worth, and people come up from the warm decks just to feel it. It's the nearest thing the drum has to an evening chill.
Night swimming is allowed until eleven. The water is warmer than the air, and climbing out into heliox is a short, loud lesson in why everyone brings a robe.

A woodwarden takes a late group into the dim wood with one hand lamp held low. Nobody speaks. In a clearing the warden switches the lamp off, and you all stand in the dark listening to the drum breathe.
Pavilions stay lit late for people who come up after work, a few hundred spread over the lawns, sitting in twos and talking quietly, as though the whole Hollow were a reading room.
Mowers come out at night: low, patient machines working the lawns in long stripes, each with a small red lamp on its back so nobody trips over it.
A child is flying a kite at night with a hand lamp tied to its tail, running long loops across the meadow to keep it up, with a small crowd of other children running behind.
Locked at night, the orchard has a low gate, and the warden dozing in a chair beside it has clearly decided not to notice anyone under twelve.
At night you can look straight up at the line at last: a dark spar nearly three kilometres long, and at each end a flying hall lit up like an open door.
Without the crowds the Hollow sounds different. You can hear water moving somewhere under the lake path, and far off, on an end-wall terrace, a choir going over the same four bars.
The couple on the next bench are deciding whether to marry, very quietly, and the heliox brings every word across. You get up and move, which is polite, and also too late.
On the lawn a man is teaching his daughter spinward and anti in the dark. He drops a cup on the grass, she feels for it, finds it a little anti of where it should be, and says 'anti' before he can.
Toward lamp-dawn the hand lamps start to gather at the two ends of the axis, where the lifts are, as the flyers come in for the night.
A few people sit up on the top terrace at lamp-night, wrapped in blankets, nearly weightless, with their feet hooked under the bench rail so they stay put when they laugh.
In the bamboo grove the night lamps are low and blue, and strips of paper hang from the culms, each with a name on it: the families' dead, renewed every year, turning slightly when anyone walks past.

Late at night the Hollow belongs to mowers and people who can't sleep. A woman jogs the lake path with a lamp on her forehead, and every lap she passes the same old man on the same bench, and they nod.
By night the great square is lit in colour, a different scheme every evening, drawn by lot from the residents' designs, and people come up just to stand in it.
A night warden's lamp comes swinging along the path. The guest hour ended at ten, the warden says kindly, and walks you all the way to the pavilion, talking about the pears.
From the meadow you can watch the flyers overhead: a long line of hand lamps moving along the axis, and now and then one that wanders off crosswise and is towed slowly back by a friend.
Night picnics are a custom here: bread, cheese, a flask of something hot, and a hand lamp in the middle of the cloth where the main dish would go.
In a thin drum the Hollow stays open all night in turns, and at three in the morning the lawns are as full as noon, with people asleep in rows under the path lamps.
Overhead, on the far bank, there's a party in a lit pavilion: tiny upside-down dancers, and then, about five seconds behind them, very faintly, the music.
Someone on the far bank is signalling with a hand lamp: on, off, on. Someone on your bank answers. They don't appear to know each other, and they keep it up for half an hour.
The Hollow closes at midnight. Wardens walk the lawns with lamps, saying 'Midnight' quietly to each little group, and nobody argues, since their deck will be back in eight weeks.

An elder on the terrace bench, wrapped up against the cool, is watching the flyers. She flew the length of the Spindle every night of the year she was twenty, she tells you, and has the knees to show for it.
{painter} sits on the back terrace at lamp-night with a slate and a cold cup of tea, sketching tomorrow's dawn in coloured lines, rubbing them out, and sketching them again.
A woman sits at the end of the jetty with her feet in the water and a hand lamp in her lap, singing to herself. Heliox carries it all the way to the bamboo, where somebody joins in.
With the line dark, the floor is lit only by its path lamps, and the paths on either side climb away as threads of light and meet again overhead.
After midnight the dim wood is open to anyone with a lamp and nothing to say. A slate at the gate reads: YOU ARE NOT LOST. KEEP WALKING.
At the cab pavilion a sleepy attendant is polishing the lift doors with great care, and asks if you saw the flyers tonight, as though they had been put on for you.

spindle: The Spindle lift climbs the end wall past the terraces, and your weight drains out as it goes. Near the top the cabin swings until down points sideways, then away altogether, and the doors open on a hall full of people swimming in the air.
Wing-sleeves are fabric fins from wrist to hip. The attendant at the gate checks your straps twice, and for the first minute you look like someone holding out a coat for somebody very tall.
Your teacher is nine. She calls you 'big aunt', shows you how to cup the air on the downstroke, and laughs, kindly, every time you hit the net.
Along the axis, flying is easy: push off, sweep, glide, and the far end of the hall comes to meet you in a straight line, as if the drum had stopped turning just for you.
Crosswise is the hard way. Fly across the axis and the drum turns under you: at a good pace you drift twenty metres in ten seconds and come out a long way from where you aimed, to applause.
On your fourth crosswise run you come out exactly at the hoop, and the whole flying hall claps. They clap for every grown-up's first hoop. It still counts.
Nobody weighs anything at the axis itself. Twenty metres out you weigh about as much as a cup of tea, and at seventy-five metres about as much as a bag of shopping, which is where the nets begin.
The hardest thing to learn isn't flying, it's stopping. You come at the end wall far too fast, flail, and are caught by a nine-year-old who has been waiting for exactly this.
By day the flying hall's light is soft and comes from below, from every side at once: the Hollow's own glow, thrown back up off a floor a kilometre and a half away all round.
Everything is below you up here. The floor curls all the way round, a kilometre and a half off in every direction, so the near bank and the far bank are the same distance down.
At lamp-night the whole Spindle opens. You fly out of the hall past the end of the nets, into the dark, with nothing ahead but nearly four kilometres of air and other people's hand lamps.
At night the sunline is a dark cable down the middle of the air. Flyers keep a polite distance from it out of daytime habit, though it stays cold until dawn.
A hand lamp weighs nothing up here and lights almost nothing. Its job is to tell other flyers where you are, and in the dark, nearly two kilometres from the nearest wall, that's the whole job.
Drift outward and you get slowly heavier, a feeling like the start of a fall that never quite gets going. Two sweeps of the sleeves bring you back in, light as before.
A girl of six goes past you crosswise on purpose, aiming well wide, and arrives at the hoop with the bored face of an expert. Some drums teach crosswise before reading.
Every child's first word up here is 'net'. Every grown-up's is something worse.
The hired sleeves have been mended so often the fins are three colours, and the darn on the left one is shaped, if you squint, like a boot.

Remade wing-sleeves cost about eighteen kays: three hundred grams of new cloth and a few hours of a maker's time. You try a pair on at the stall by the gate, fly a little way to be sure, and that's how it starts.
Two people can hold hands and fly the length of the hall together, and half the couples in the drum say that's how they started.
The gate attendant asks if you've flown before, looks at your face, and hands you the sleeves with the biggest fins.
Flying in heliox is quiet. The sleeves make a soft fluttering hiss, and people's voices reach you bright and small from a long way off.
An old man in patched sleeves flies past very slowly along the axis, reading.
At the hoop line the teacher counts you in, three, two, one, and you push off the post and swim for it, and the drum, turning under you, carries the hoop politely out of the way.
Night flyers keep to the right along the axis, two slow streams of hand lamps going opposite ways, and anyone crossing between them is cheered or scolded depending on how it goes.

Halfway along the Spindle at night you stop sweeping and just hang there, nearly two kilometres from either end, with the dark cable beside you, and for a while nothing in the drum is touching you at all.
Crosswise, the drift doesn't feel like anything. You fly straight, as far as your body can tell, and the hall simply slides sideways while you aren't looking.
There's a moment in every first flight when you stop sweeping and nothing happens, and you realise nothing is going to: no falling, no floor, just you and the air, going on.
A nine-year-old offers to race you along the axis, and you lose by half the hall. The rematch is crosswise, and you lose by a different half.
The nets at the ends of the flying hall are soft, wide and well used. Every so often a whole class flies into them in a row, on purpose, just for the feel of it.
From the axis the end wall looks like the inside of a bowl, tier on tier going down and out, and every person standing on it has their head pointed straight at you.
At lamp-night a choir flies the Spindle, forty singers strung out along the axis, and the heliox carries their voices out to both banks at once.
A sweep with both arms drives you forward. A sweep with one sets you slowly turning, end over end, until a passing child takes your ankle and stops you without comment.
Hired sleeves come with a hand lamp and a little card of rules. The last rule reads: IF YOU ARE LOST, FLY ALONG. YOU WILL REACH AN END.
Crosswise lessons happen in the slack hour after lunch, when the hall is half empty and there's room to come out somewhere you didn't mean to.

At lamp-night a family flies the Spindle together: the parents lengthwise and steady, the children looping round them crosswise, drifting off and being fetched back, over and over, the whole way along.
Coming down in the lift afterwards your weight returns a little at every terrace, and by the floor your arms feel as though they belong to someone heavier.
Children who grew up flying stand a particular way when they're nervous, arms held a little out from their sides, as if checking for sleeves.
At the axis there's no up. The teacher tells you to pick one, any one, and fly toward it, and after that it's yours for the afternoon.
Flyers in a hurry go along. Flyers in love go crosswise, slowly, so they can drift.
The teacher says sleeves aren't wings, they're bigger hands, and makes you swim the length of the hall with your fingers spread until you believe it.
Now and then an attendant has to fetch somebody who has stopped dead in the middle of the hall and forgotten how to start again. It takes a long pole and no comment.
At three in the morning the Spindle is nearly empty: a few lamps along the axis, the floor's path lamps all round, and somewhere an elder flying slow lengths alone, as regular as a swimmer.
At lamp-night the edge of flying country is marked by a ring of small green lamps seventy-five metres out from the axis. Past them, the floor starts wanting you back.
You can always tell who learned in a crosswise drum: they turn into every crossing early, aiming at a spot well to one side of where they want to be, and arrive exactly.
A teacher of about nine hands you a hand lamp and says, 'Don't drop it.' Then, watching it hang beside your fingers: 'Well. You can't, really.'

window.t: Up the back wall in the Spindle lift, past the terraces, the weight drains out of you. Near the top the cabin swings until down points sideways, then toward the axis, then nowhere at all.
The back axle hall is the loudest place in the drum. Pipes as wide as rooms carry its heat out as ammonia, a river's worth, through the great rotary joint into the part of the raft that doesn't turn.
A guide meets the group at the axle: a young woman with a soft voice who has done this a thousand times and talks to each eight-year-old as though this were her first.
Every other grown-up in the group came with a child. An eight-year-old asks who you brought, and when you say nobody, thinks it over and lends you a hand to hold for the float in.

For a while the chamber turns with the drum. Then, slowly, it stops turning, or the drum does: for a little under two minutes you watch the whole axle hall wheel round you once, and then you're in the part of the raft where nothing turns.
A short armoured car takes you out along a shielded track through the radiator layer. It has no windows, which the children find very funny for about a minute.
Every child in the car holds a hand-strap with both hands, as though zero g might change its mind. Their adults hold the children.
Past the rotary joint the noise falls away, and the quiet of the still part of the raft is so sudden that a child laughs out loud just to hear something.
In the despin chamber everyone is told to hold a strap and look at the wall. Nobody looks at the wall. Everybody watches the hall go round.
One last rule before the car: no lamps, no screens, nothing that glows. A father quietly takes off his watch and puts it in his pocket, face in.
For a few long, quiet minutes the track runs out through the radiator layer. The guide tells the children that the back of the raft is out there, very cold and very big, which seems to satisfy them.
At the far end of the track there's a hatch, a short tunnel and a heavy curtain, and the guide holds the curtain aside with one hand and says, 'In you float.'

Inside it's dim and red: a long low gallery, couches in tiers, a shutter along one wall. You strap in, because nothing here weighs anything, and wait with a hundred and fifty people who are all trying to whisper.
Twenty minutes in the red light, the guide says, because eyes need that long to wake up to the dark, and nobody wants to waste their one time.
In the red light every face is the same colour, and the eight-year-old strapped in beside you has decided you're the person to tell everything to. You learn a great deal about spinball.
A device lights up in someone's pocket, and the whole gallery groans, softly, in a hundred and fifty heliox voices. The guide adds five minutes to the wait so everyone's eyes can forgive it.
Nobody looks anywhere but the shutter: long, low, very plain, a grey wall with a seam down its length. Everyone in the gallery is looking at the seam.
Behind you an old man tells his granddaughter what he saw when he was eight. He has it wrong, you'll find out in a few minutes, but he has it gently.
A child near the front falls asleep during the wait and has to be woken, and wakes furious. It's a long wait for something you've been told about all your life.
Slowly your eyes change. The red light that seemed so dim at first is almost bright now, and the guide's face comes up out of it, smiling.
The guide says the shutter will open slowly, that nobody needs to say anything, and then, very quietly, starts counting down from ten.
There's no near star at all. What fills the Window instead is the River: a broad band of stars right across the sky, more than anyone could count, pale gold, the brightest of them orange.
Thick and bright in the middle, the River frays at its edges, with dark rifts of dust lying across it. Where the dust thins, its edges go brown-violet. The crews call that colour bruise.
Above and below the River hangs a fainter glow, the Shelf, so faint you see it best by looking just beside it.
Nothing twinkles. The stars simply sit there, steady as print, as if the sky were a page someone had been very careful with.
Here and there are places where nothing shines at all: black shapes, from specks to one about a fingernail wide at arm's length. 'Rafts,' says the guide. About a sixth of the sky is rafts.
'Watch the edge of the big one,' says the guide, 'by that orange star.' It takes most of an hour. Then the black edge creeps over the star, and the star goes out.
Nobody in the gallery says anything for a long time: a hundred and fifty people breathing, and not one of them asking for anything.
Beside you, a girl counts stars under her breath, gets to forty, stops, and doesn't start again.
Your eyes keep waking. Ten minutes after the shutter opens there are twice as many stars as there were, and ten minutes after that the dark between them isn't empty either.
This light left the River centuries ago, before the oldest chair you know was a tree.
One of the black shapes is a thin sliver, a raft seen almost edge-on, laid across the River like a dropped thread.
In the dark you hear the adults more than the children: a breath caught, someone's 'oh', a father quietly saying a child's name for no reason except to say it.
A small boy holds his hand up against the dark and measures a black shape with his fingers: one finger, two. 'That one's ours,' he says, which it isn't, and nobody corrects him.
The River runs the whole length of the shutter and keeps going past both ends, and you catch yourself leaning, uselessly, to see the rest.
'We used to bet on those,' says an old woman a few couches along, watching a raft's edge close on a star. She doesn't say whether she won.
Far down the River the guide points out a raft so distant it's only a missing star, a gap in the grain, and says its children are probably being brought to look this way.

On the way back the guide tells the children where the metal comes from: the River, where stars are taken apart and sorted and the metal sent inward to fall for a million years. Their couches, their sleeves, every bit of them heavier than helium, fell out of that.
Back in the part of the raft where nothing turns, the children are very quiet, and then all at once very loud.
Going down the back wall, the lift gives your weight back a little at a time, and by the floor it feels heavier than it did this morning, as though you'd brought something back with you.
At the hall that night everyone asks what it was like, and you can't say. You try 'gold' and 'a lot' and give up, and the cook nods as if that were the right answer.
At the next wedding you go to, someone will cut the apple crosswise and hold up the star of seeds, and now you'll know what it's a picture of.

In bed that night you turn the lamp all the way off, lie on your back and wait for your eyes to wake. Nothing comes, of course, but you know exactly where the River is now: past the end of the drum, behind the radiators.
An eight-year-old from the gallery spots you on the platform next morning and waves with great seriousness, as one veteran to another.
The iron in your blood, the guide said, fell out of that. All afternoon you keep catching yourself touching your wrist.
Every child gets a card at the hatch with the gallery's name and the date. There's one left over at the end, and the guide gives it to you.

backcrew.t: Before the shift you sign for the dose: one sheet, one small number, and a crew chief who reads it out loud to make sure you heard. Then a badge goes on your chest, and stays there all day.
Suiting up takes most of an hour. The visor looks aft, away from the Lantern side of everything, so for eight hours the sky will be over your shoulder whether you look or not.
A back crew takes a guest the way you'd take a nephew to work: a job to hold, a list of things not to touch, and a great deal of teasing before the hatch.
Out through the axle, past the rotary joint, into the part of the raft that doesn't turn, then a long ride on a cold shielded track to the crew hatch, where the radiators begin.
Everything is tied to something. Your tools are on lanyards, the lanyards are on you, you're on the sled, and the crew chief checks every clip twice and yours three times.
{name}, the crew's oldest hand, says the trick is to look at the work for the first hour before you look at anything else. Nobody manages it, {name} included.
Zero g in a suit is nothing like zero g on a cycler. Every move you make, the suit makes a moment later and slightly differently, like a large, polite friend.
The sled runs along the panel row on its rail, and the panels go on in every direction, grey and dull, until the dark swallows them. The crew calls this one a short row.
An ammonia leak shows as a glittering fan of crystals, pretty enough that you watch it for a moment before remembering it's a fault. The crew chief, who has seen thousands, watches it too.
You hold the pump while {name2} swears at it. The swearing is long, inventive and oddly tender, and at the end of it the pump comes away.
Changing a pump takes two hours and four people, three of whom are needed. You're the fourth. You're given the bag of fittings, and you guard it with your life.
A puncture is a hole the width of a pencil, and patching it takes twenty minutes and a great deal of quiet. When it's done, the crew chief pats the patch twice, like a shoulder.
Radio talk out here is mostly numbers and mild insults. Halfway through the shift someone asks how the guest is doing, and three voices answer before you can.
Lunch is broth through a straw inside the helmet, lukewarm and salty, and it's the best broth you've had all year, which the crew says every guest says.
Under the sled, the panels carry the heat of two hundred million people out into the dark as light no eye can see. The crew says you can feel it through a glove if you're patient, and you aren't.
Down the row a cracked coupling has grown a little white beard of its own frozen ammonia. The crew calls it exactly that, a beard, and somebody is sent to shave it.
All shift the whole sky is over your shoulder: the River right across it, pale gold, the Shelf above and below, and the black shapes of rafts where nothing shines.
Where the River's dust thins, its edges go brown-violet. The crew calls that colour bruise, and says it the way you'd say the name of a neighbour.
The crew bets on occultations. A raft's edge is closing on an orange star, and by mid-shift there are eleven small bets on the minute it goes out, one of them yours.
The old hands hardly look up. Then, at the end of a job, every one of them does, for a moment, the way you'd glance out of a window you've had all your life.
Turning on the sled, you get the River full in your visor and forget for a second which way the work is. 'Everyone does that,' says a voice on the radio. 'For about forty years.'
Bigger rafts get names, the way a hall names its regulars: the Thumb, the Long One, Old Square. Nobody knows what the people on them call themselves.
Nobody out here says 'stars' much. They say the River and the Shelf and bruise and that one there, and point with a gloved hand you can only just see.
Sometime after lunch a star by the edge of a black raft goes out, the radio goes quiet, and then someone says 'Pay up', and everyone groans except {name}, who won.
Back inside, the badge is read and the dose logged, and the crew chief reads the number out like a score. It's small. Everyone claps anyway.
On the lift down the weight comes back a little at every terrace, and every muscle you used to hold that pump writes in to complain.
At the hatch they give you a patch: a square of cloth with a band of tiny stitched stars across it. 'One shift,' says the chief, 'so don't go wearing it on the front.'
After the shift there's a cup of something hot in the crew room, and nobody talks about the sky. They talk about the pump, at length, with love.
That night you sleep eleven hours and dream, all of it, about holding things.
As you leave, the crew chief says you did well, which you know is said to everyone, and then that you held the bag well, which you suspect isn't.

nights.t: Whoever stayed here last kept the herb shelf going under its little lamp: basil, shiso, and a clump of chives cut short by a hundred wanderers. The label on the pot says take what you need, it grows back.

On the table is a note from the last wanderer: the left tap runs hot, the chair by the door is better than it looks, and the woman on {street} sells the best buns on the deck. You'll add a line of your own before you go.
The guest book is three books tied together with string. The oldest entries are in a hand you can barely read, and one of them says exactly what you were about to write.
Your chair has been mended so often that the mends have mends, each in a different thread, all of them shown on purpose. It's the most comfortable thing you've sat on all year.

A neighbour knocks at nine with a lidded bowl: too much stew, she says, and a guest is the best excuse. The bowl goes back to her door in the morning with a sprig of something in it, which is apparently how it's done.
Through the wall someone is practising a heliox flute, the same four bars over and over. On the ninth time a neighbour knocks twice, and the flute stops mid-note.

A little after one the laundry machines start up somewhere below, when the kays are cheapest, and the whole block gives a low, contented rumble. It's three thousand people's shirts, and you sleep through the rest.

Until a month ago this flat was lent to {name} and {name2}, a young couple waiting for a place of their own. They've left five apple seeds in a dish on the shelf, set out in a star, and a note: from the wedding, for luck.

The flat's last long-term tenant was a lamp-painter, and it shows: the room lamp has nine settings, each named in tiny handwriting on the switch plate. You try them all before bed, and settle on one called the long gold.
The flat is set warmer than you'd keep it, and a card by the controls says: guests always turn it down, and then they turn it back up. You turn it down. At two in the morning you turn it back up.
Empty Margin on either side, kept for whoever needs it next, so the only neighbour you have tonight is the drum itself: fans, pumps, water, and two hundred million people breathing.

{block}'s block court is meeting in the atrium below, and its voices come up through the floor: a long, good-natured fight over whether the atrium's light should go to the floor or the terraces. The terraces are losing, by the sound of it, as they have for years.
You drop a spoon in the kitchen and it lands a finger's width antispinward, and you hear yourself say 'anti' like a child. Nobody's there to hear it, which is a relief.
Water from the hot tap comes out at sixty-five degrees and boils in about a minute. You make tea with a sprig off the guest shelf and drink it sitting up in bed, which feels like a crime and isn't.

Someone called {name} has left a long letter on the table, sealed, addressed to whoever stays here next, to be read once. It's about a reel on the terraces forty years ago, and you read it once, slowly.
Made of other quilts, the quilt on the bed has a tag sewn into one corner listing eleven owners and the drums they came from, with room left for more.

At 23:00 the lamps fade and the drum seems to lower its voice with them. Out in the corridor someone says goodnight to someone else, and the heliox brings it through the door as clearly as if it were meant for you.
With the black thread on your wrist and your worlds switched off, the flat is quiet enough to hear the herb shelf's little lamp click off at midnight. You hadn't known it did that.

The block has left a welcome: a heel of sourdough under a cloth, a jar of the Nine, and a card from a {block} table saying breakfast is at seven and nobody will mind if you're late. Somebody will mind a little, the card adds.

This flat is kept for refuge as well as for guests, and the cupboard is stocked for both: soft clothes in three sizes, a larder shelf, a slate with the clinic's hours. You use none of it, and you're glad it's there.

On the doorframe are pencil lines with heights and dates, none of the names the same. Wanderers have been measuring themselves against it for years, and one has written beside theirs: taller after the slow line, won't last.
Labels on the herb shelf, in a dozen hands: BASIL, ALSO BASIL, NOT BASIL (SHISO), and in fresh ink, PLEASE WATER.
From the flat you can hear the {block} hall two decks down putting itself to bed: chairs going up on tables, a pot being scrubbed, someone singing the last verse of something to the cleaning robot.

Late in the night the flat next door opens and closes very quietly: a family on refuge, the block said, who came in yesterday. In the morning there's a child's drawing under your door of a glide car with a face in its window.
The guest flat is plain and very clean: a bed, a chair, a lamp, exactly three herb pots and a card with the Mill Hall's hours. It's like being looked after by someone who doesn't want to make a fuss.
Inside the door are {drum}'s house rules for guests, all of them reasonable except the last, which says guests may not take a resident's Hollow hour. Someone has written underneath: we tried.

No Margin here, just a row of six guest rooms on a Low deck, kept since before anyone's grandmother, and tonight you're the only guest. Someone has left all six lamps on so the corridor won't feel empty, which is a kindness.
The last guest left a pair of knitted slippers by the bed with a tag: for cold feet, any size, leave them for the next one. They're too big and very warm.
Stiff, shiny and nobody's grandmother's, the chair in the guest flat is the newest thing you've seen in a week. You sit in it anyway, and feel a bit sorry for it.
Upstairs someone paces for an hour, and at nine-tenths of a g every step comes through the ceiling. At midnight the pacing stops, a baby cries once, and the pacing starts again, gentler.
The guest register asks two questions: where from, and where next. In the where-next column, the guest before you has written: home, slowly.
Right below the guest flat is the Mill Hall, and at a quarter to six you wake to the smell of jook and the clank of the big lids going on. It is, you have to admit, a good way to wake up.
Someone has turned the sheets sides to middle, the old way of making them last, and the seam down the centre lies perfectly flat. That's care, taken for a stranger.

Two old neighbours are playing a game in the corridor outside, on a board older than both of them, and every few minutes one of them says 'oh, no' with enormous satisfaction. You fall asleep before finding out who wins.

Your host gift, a sprig from your own shelf, sits in a glass of water on the guest flat's shelf because there was nobody to give it to. In the morning you give it to the Mill Hall cook, who is more pleased than it deserves.

Next door to the guest flat are the baths, and all night you can hear the water: warm from the food plant's loop, moving slowly, now and then a pipe ticking as it settles. It's like sleeping beside someone's kettle.
There's no herb shelf in the guest flat, which seems so wrong that you check twice. A note explains that it's being re-potted, and apologises at some length.
Like most rooms in a drum, the guest flat on deck {deck} has no window, just a painted panel of a pear tree where one would be. It's been repainted at least twice, and each time the pears got bigger.
A stack of books by the bed was left by other guests, each with a ticket where someone stopped reading when their three nights ran out. You finish one of them for a stranger.
Two guests share the flat tonight: you, and a wanderer from {far} going the other way round the raft. You swap broth rankings until one of you falls asleep mid-sentence.
At six exactly a warm roll drops through the bread slot in the door and lands on the mat. You weren't expecting it, and you'll remember this drum for it.

Sleeping a few decks above the Keel, you can feel the drum at work through the bed: the slow beat of the pumps, the Mill turning over, the lamp-night running on machines. It's oddly like being rocked.

No guest-right in this drum, so you take a room at an inn on {street}, down on the Low decks, for three kays a night, breakfast extra. The innkeeper takes the kays almost apologetically, as if guest-right were something she'd personally failed to provide.

Low decks are where the drum keeps its families, and the inn sits among them: school bags in the corridor, a spinball thudding against a wall somewhere, a child refusing to go to bed in a voice that carries three doors.
Felt on every wall stops the corridor's noise at your door like a well-brought-up visitor. Inside there's only your own pulse and the faint push of the vent.

{name}, who keeps the inn, is past ninety and runs it mostly by sitting at the desk and knowing things: which cab core is quickest to the Hollow, which lake bench gets the best of the dawn. Both answers turn out to be right.
Your room has a real window, onto a block's atrium, and you lie awake for an hour watching the lamps in other people's kitchens go out one by one.
Breakfast is included if you're up by seven and not if you're not, and the innkeeper's son explains this to you with great seriousness at half past seven.
Through the thin wall you hear a couple next door planning their whole wedding in whispers, which in heliox are not whispers at all. By midnight you have opinions about the seating.
Four kays a night is more than the glide, the broth and the cab put together, and the innkeeper knows it. There's a slice of cake on the pillow to make up the difference.

The inn is full of commuters who missed the last glide home to {nb}, and they treat it like a dormitory: shoes in a row, one kettle, a long letter read aloud to the room at midnight because nobody can sleep.
Heavy sheets, a heavy quilt and nine-tenths of a g: you lie in the inn's bed like a pressed flower and don't move until morning.

Spirits are taxed hard here, so the inn keeps a single bottle of gin under the counter and pours it like medicine. A glass costs about what dinner did, and the innkeeper watches you drink it as though it were a performance.
Rooms here are named, not numbered, after the drums the innkeepers came from, and you've been put in {nb}. It has the best bed, apparently, though every room says that about itself.

An inn on the Low decks is where a drum keeps its strangers: freight crews, wedding guests, a man selling flutes, two wanderers and you. Breakfast is at one long table, because nobody ever built a second.
Thousands of travellers have slept in this bed, and the mattress remembers the average of them: a long, shallow dip the shape of nobody in particular. You fit it surprisingly well.

The night porter does the rounds at two with a hand lamp, checking doors, and pauses at yours long enough to whisper, 'All right?' In heliox it reaches your pillow as clearly as if it had been said from the end of the bed.
Behind the desk a board lists everyone staying tonight by first name and drum. You're the only one from yours, so the innkeeper has written it very large, as if you were a delegation.
The bunk is still warm when you climb in: its other sleeper went on shift ten minutes ago and left a note on the pillow. Sleep well, it says, I'm back at six.

Your hot-bunk has a curtain, a reading lamp the size of a thumb and a shelf with three things on it, none of them yours. The rules on the card: lamp off at midnight, curtain shut, no eating in bed, and in another hand, everyone eats in bed.
On the rota by the door, in fresh chalk, is your name: the bunk by the water pipe, ten till six. A woman on her way to work taps it as she passes and says, 'Good bunk. Warm in the night.'

Twelve bunks in a room built for four, and the twelve people in them are the politest you've ever slept beside. Someone snores; someone else reaches over and rolls him onto his side without either of them waking.
Nobody in this drum has a room to themselves, and nobody seems to think they should. Your bunk-mate on the day shift, {name}, has left you half a pastry and a book open at a good bit.
Four other curtains went into the one round your bunk, sewn together very finely, and someone has embroidered a little glide car in one corner for luck.
Lights out isn't a thing here, because someone in the room is always going to work or coming back. The lamps stay low all night, and you sleep the way everyone does, with an arm across your eyes.
The family whose bunk you share by shifts have given you the good blanket and refuse to discuss it. In the morning you find they've also mended the tear in your bag.

Night in a full drum is a long hallway of breathing: eight sleepers in your room, twenty through the wall, and somewhere a child telling a younger one a story. In heliox you can hear every word, and it's a good story.
Above you sleeps a man who has done this for {years} years and has a system: earplugs, a sock over the lamp, a hand lamp clipped to the slats so he can find the ladder. He lends you the earplugs.

You're on the night rota, so you sleep through the middle of the day in a room of other day-sleepers, felt on the walls and the corridor's day going on outside the door. It's oddly peaceful, like napping at the edge of a party.

At shift change the whole room stirs at once, one lot getting up and the other getting in, two dozen people passing through a space for eight without an elbow. You lie very still and learn how it's done.
Someone in the room is homesick, quietly, and the room handles it the way it handles everything: a hand on a shoulder going past, a cup of broth left by the bunk, nobody saying a word.
A sign over the bunks says: this drum is full, and you are welcome. Under it, smaller: so is the Mill Hall, from six.

Your sleeping bag is clipped to the wall at shoulders and feet, and when you let go, your arms float up in front of you like a sleepwalker's. Everyone on the slow line sleeps like that. You stop noticing on the third night.

A little fan by your head keeps your own breath from pooling round your face, as it would all night with nothing to carry it off. You fall asleep to its hush and dream you're walking somewhere, on a floor.
The train never stops. At two in the morning it's still doing two kilometres a second, and the only sign of it is a faint steady sound in the wall that may be the air, or the train, or you.

Something drifts past your face in the dark: a sock, yours, escaped from its net. By morning it'll be stuck to the air intake with everyone else's lost things, which is where the slow line keeps its lost property.

There's no up in the sleeping car, so the riders have agreed on one: the Galley end is down. Two new riders who didn't know have clipped themselves in head toward the floor, and look perfectly comfortable.
At lamp-night the car's lights go to a dim red, and the riders go quiet one sleeping bag at a time, the way the lamps go down along a street at home.
The rider in the next bag talks in their sleep, a whole conversation in a {farrow} accent, with pauses in the right places. It sounds like a call home with the light delay left in.
You wake not knowing which way you're facing, because there isn't a way. It takes a minute to find the wall, the light, your own hands, and then the smell of the stockpot drifting from the Galley.
Somewhere in the night the light delay home changes by another quarter of a second. You can't feel it, and you check anyway.
Every hour the night rider at the Galley gives the stockpot's crank a slow turn, so it never sits. Around three its smell reaches the sleeping car, and half the bags stir and settle again.
Someone's bungee cord has come loose in the night and drifts across the car in a slow, purposeful curl. Nobody gets up. In the morning it's wrapped round the Galley door like a ribbon on a present.
Nine nights clipped to a wall, and tonight, for the first time, you don't hold on to anything to fall asleep. Your hands just float, palms up, as if waiting to be given something.
In the sleeping car it's quiet enough to hear a pencil float out of someone's pocket, tap the wall once, and slowly come back.

Before sleep the riders write their long letters, each in a bag with a clip-light, scratching away like students the night before an exam. The letters go home by light, the only thing on this line in a hurry.
Your hair floats round your head all night, and you wake with some of it in your mouth. The rider opposite, {name}, recommends a net and shows you one that's clearly older than its owner.

Around midnight a capsule docks with a soft thump through the whole train, and then someone new comes floating up the corridor in the dark, apologising to every sleeping bag. By morning they'll know everyone's name.

The Galley's night lamp stays on for whoever can't sleep, and at three there are four of you round the stockpot, holding bulbs of broth and talking low about home. Nobody asks anyone's name until morning.

Weightless sleep is the deepest you've had all year, with nothing pressing on any part of you. Waking is the strange bit: for a moment you don't know where your body ends, and then you find your feet, a long way off.

quiet: The Quiet starts when the lamps come up. Every world in {drum} goes off at once, and by eight the halls are full of people holding cups and nothing else.

With the worlds off, the drum sounds different: no chimes, nobody laughing at something you can't see, only voices and the fans. An old man at the next table says it's the one day a year he can hear the tea being poured.

Nobody plans what to talk about on the Quiet. By noon your table has covered the atrium's light, a cousin's wedding, the right way to fold a dumpling and whether the beam will be flat, which it nearly always is.
Children last about an hour before they stop asking for their worlds. By afternoon they've built a spinball league out of chairs and a rolled-up sock, and the aunts are refereeing badly on purpose.

On the hall wall someone keeps the tally as the day goes: every dark wallet in the block, a little over nine kays a head, adding up toward tomorrow's feast. When it's enough for a steak each, somebody draws a steak.

You were told the Quiet was a fast, and it feels like the opposite: eleven hours at a long table, more talk than you've had in a month, and a stranger who knows your home drum's broth and thinks it's wrong.
The old bring out their long letters on the Quiet, the kind written to be read once, and read them aloud to whoever sits down. A letter read in the Quiet, they say, counts as answered.
Late in the evening the hall goes soft. Someone lifts a flute as long as a broom, nobody tells it to stop, and two hundred people listen to a thing nobody is recording.
booking: At ten the booking arrives: Merrow's beam for the year ahead, flat, as it nearly always is. The hall cheers anyway, because cheering a flat year is the point.

The Ledger is read aloud at the station ring: shares, people, the Margin, places, births and deaths, and then the names, each newborn beside the dead whose share they carry. Families stand for their own line and sit down again quickly, a little embarrassed.

The assembly by lot reads its split from the hall steps, and then the one question everyone votes on: another hour of full sunline, or a bigger hall fund. Guests can't vote, so three different people tell you how you would have.

The feast is the Quiet's savings on a plate: a cultivated steak each, a salad cut generously for once, aged cheese, wine, and an orchard apple cut crosswise for every two people so everyone sees the star.
Your plate is the same as everyone else's, paid for by a Quiet you weren't even here for. When you try to say so, the cook puts more cheese on it.
The vote comes in late in the afternoon: the hall fund, by a few points. The losing side announces that the sunline will win next year and goes back for more cheese.
At your table the knife goes to the youngest, who cuts the apple crooked. The star comes out lopsided, and it's declared the luckiest one in the hall.
The cook's Booking toast is short: the beam is booked, the larders are full, and nobody at this table will be cold or dim this year. Then the lids come off.
By mid-afternoon the halls run out of plates and start on bowls, then cups. A small boy eats his salad with his fingers because it's Booking Day, and nobody stops him.
On the way out people touch the old Count board that hangs beside the Ledger, the one from before the Margin. Nobody explains it to guests, and nobody needs to.
longflight: At ten the sunline stays dark and the Spindle opens end to end. From the back terraces you watch the first hand lamps go up, a few, then a slow river of them along the axis toward the far wall.
Up at the axis you weigh nothing, and the line you'd keep well away from by day is a dark cable down the middle of the air. Flyers pass along it all night, lamps held out, faces lit from below.
The flight runs in shifts by block until lamp-dawn. Your hosts have the two o'clock shift, so you sleep in your clothes with the borrowed sleeves folded on the chair.
Somewhere ahead in the lamps a choir is flying and singing at once, high and bright in heliox, the words lost and the tune not.

Crosswise in the dark is how people lose their block. You spend twenty minutes drifting through strangers' lamps asking for {block}, everyone points a different way, and all of them are kind about it.
Old people watch from the elders' terrace with a glass of gin each and agree it was better the year they flew it. Every year, it was better the year they flew it.
Couples fly holding wrists, which turns them slowly end over end whenever one of them flaps harder. Half the Long Flight is couples tumbling gently along the axis, laughing.
Hundreds of thousands of people in the air and almost no noise: the sleeves make a soft sound like a sheet being shaken out, and in the middle of the Spindle everyone, without being told, talks low.
knotnight: On Knotnight the atrium lamps go down to almost nothing at seven, and the whole block makes the year's larder by hand lamp: hard bread, jars of pickle, miso, noodles hung to dry across broom handles.

Every jar gets a knot of string round its neck and a label with the year. Nobody agrees what the knot is for; the oldest woman in the block says it's so you can find the jar in the dark, and nobody argues with her.

The rule is to eat whatever's fresh, as if a long dark were coming. So the salad that would have lasted the week goes tonight, all of it, and a tomato goes round the table in slices on the end of a knife.
Children are given the Nine to tin, because nothing can spoil it. They taste it anyway, every one of them, and make the face.
Somebody always tells the Eleven Days on Knotnight. The ones who were children then remember the dark as the best game they ever played; the ones who were parents mostly listen.
Last year's hard bread is soaked in this year's broth and eaten as a treat, which everyone pretends it is until, round about midnight, it is.
You're handed a jar to fill, and it goes into a stranger's larder with your home drum's name on the label. Someone in {drum} will open it in a hard year and wonder who you were.
At midnight the lamps come back up and everyone blinks at what they've made: a few hundred jars along the atrium tables, every one knotted, every one with a name.
passing: The Passing has begun: another raft within a couple of AU, near enough to talk to. The hall choir sends a round at seven and then sits, waiting, through thirty-three minutes of nothing.
Thirty-three minutes is long enough for dinner. The choir eats in its robes and is back on the risers, still chewing, when the answer starts.
Their voices come back in their own heliox, a little different from ours, brighter at the top or just shaped by ages of singing apart. Nobody in the hall moves until the last note.
Tonight's passing-raft menu is a soup whose recipe left the other raft's kitchens seventeen minutes before it reached ours. The cooks have it on the tables within the hour, and argue about the salt.

The other raft sends a bread with its starter as a file. The strain library will grow the culture back from its genome in about a week, so the bakers spend the week arguing about what it will taste like.

From the Windows the other raft is a black shape against the River, two fingers wide at arm's length. Most people never go and look; they listen to it instead, in the halls, every evening for a month.
There's a short list on the hall wall of everyone who has ever swapped across in a Passing. People read it the way they read the Ledger's names, slowly, looking for their own.

Somebody sends the other raft a recording of the block court arguing about the atrium's light. Thirty-three minutes later back comes a recording of theirs, arguing about almost exactly the same thing.

Choirs send rounds because a round survives the wait. You sing your part across the light, and half an hour later it comes back with their part folded in, two rafts singing one song seventeen light-minutes apart.
The kitchens keep a book of what came over in the last Passing. The best thing in it is a soup; the worst is a cake that won't rise in our air, and every year somebody tries again.
homecoming: A train comes in at lamp-dawn and the platform is full of hand lamps: a block meeting its wanderers home. Each one steps off into their own table, and the rest of the block holds the lamps high so the aunts can see their faces.
The ring counter does a second cup of broth for every wanderer home, the only day it does, and they drink it on the platform while their table watches as if it were a recital.
A young man has brought an orchard apple to the platform and is holding it behind his back. The whole block knows what it means, and the wanderer coming down the steps can tell from their faces.
