You watch a stranger's homecoming from the counter: forty hand lamps, a table of five, and an old woman who takes the wanderer's face in both hands and looks it over like a coat, for mends.
The Ledger by the platform keeps a line for wanderers home this year, and when it ticks up the whole block cheers as if a vote had been won.
Somebody always brings the wanderer's own herb pot, kept alive for a year by an aunt who had opinions about it. It's handed over on the platform with a list of everything it did while they were gone.

cards.t: Writing this on the platform with the broth still too hot to drink. The whole table came to see me off and they're still here, pretending they're only talking to each other. I have a crock, a hand lamp and no idea what I'm doing, which they all say is correct.
First card, and nothing has happened yet except the ring counter, which gave me a rice ball and wished me a good year as if it says that to everyone. It does. I cried anyway.
Light home: {light}. It's the last time it'll be that short, so I'm making the most of it.
The first leg costs about seven cups of coffee and takes eleven days. I've never been anywhere for eleven days. I've never really been anywhere.
You packed me a black thread, 'in case'. In case of what? I've put it in the pocket with the crock spoon, and the doors are opening, so I suppose I'll find out.
Day {day}, and I haven't even glided yet. The release is in four minutes, everyone on this platform has done this before, and every one of them looks jealous.

Glided to {drum} this morning: a hundred and forty seconds of nothing in my stomach, and through the water the drums standing in rows with their quay lights on, all the way back to nowhere. A child next to me said 'again' at the catch. Me too.

Nobody warned me the catch is the good bit. The weight comes back over a second, like someone sitting down on you kindly. An old man across the aisle held his hat on the whole way, as if it might leave him for {nb}.

I counted the rings of quay lights through the window and got to forty before they ran together into one line. Every ring's a drum and every drum is two hundred million people, and I'm writing to one of them.
The glide is the only view of outside most people ever get, and half the car looked the whole way. The other half slept. They're the ones who live here.
There was a choir on my glide, going to a wedding in {nb}, and they sang right through the free fall. The catch came in the middle of a long note and they held it.
I've lost count of the glides, and I still put my hand flat on the window at the release. A woman who glides to work every day saw me do it and said she does too.

{drum} smells of yeast near the platform, which turns out to be the Vats and not anyone baking. The ring counter's broth is thinner than ours, and I've been asked not to say so. Three nights, then on.
Day {day}. Signed in, got a key, and was shown the herb shelf by a man who made me promise to water it. I've watered it twice already; it's a very small flat and the shelf is the best thing in it.

I keep dropping things in {drum} and expecting them to land somewhere new. They land a little anti, like everywhere, because every drum turns the same way. Somehow that's the most homesick I've been all week.
People in {drum} say {nb} is louder, brighter and a little pleased with itself. I glide there on {weekday}. I'll let you know.
Every drum has one thing it tells you about before you're off the platform. {drum}'s is its broth. I've had it. I have notes.
Drum number {n}. They're all the same size, which ought to make them the same, and none of them are: this one hangs felt in every corridor, so everyone sounds as if they're telling you a secret.
Light home is {light} today. I said something to you out loud on the platform and then waited, as if you might answer.
Got in late. {drum} at night is laundry machines and somebody practising a flute three walls away, very well. I've decided to like it here.

{drum} is a hall drum: every block has one long table and somebody always cooking at it. Tonight I sat between a nurse and a nine-year-old, and both of them corrected how I held my spoon. I've never been so well fed or so loudly.
In the halls here they bang the lids when the stew comes in, every table, every night, and in heliox it's deafening. {name} says you stop hearing it after a week. {name} bangs loudest.
Guests can cook if they ask, so I asked. I made our noodles for three hundred people and only one of them said 'interesting'.

Music in {drum} is just what happens after dinner. Tonight it was a flute as long as a broom, played by a girl of eleven while the hall finished its pudding, and nobody clapped until every lid was back on. I've decided that's manners.

The cook here is seventy-something and runs the room like a choir: she points with the ladle, and fifty volunteers move. I washed pots for two hours, which guests don't have to do, and I'd do it again tomorrow.
Three nights eating in {drum}'s halls and I've started counting the chairs in every room I walk into. I think it means something. I'll tell you when I know what.
{drum} is a wood drum, and nobody talks in the woods; they carry slates. I wrote HELLO on mine and a woman wrote back SHH, and then, underneath, WELCOME.
I asked a woodwarden how old the yews were. She held up both hands, then both hands again, then gave up and smiled, which I think means very.
In the silent hall here you ask for the salt with your eyebrows. I've got quite good at it. I asked for the bread with my eyebrows and got a hug, so not that good.
Wood drums are dim on purpose: they spend their light on trees instead of squares. It took me a day to stop squinting and two to stop wanting the lamps up, and now I don't want to leave.
I wrote this card on a slate first, to practise, and wiped it. Everything I write here comes out shorter.
A man in the wood today stood under a birch for twenty minutes with his eyes shut. I thought he was unwell. He was listening to the water in the pipes under the floor, and when I tried it, so was I.
{drum} auctions its best seats for the dusk and hands the rents back to everyone who lives here. I'm a guest, so I just got the dusk. That seemed fair to me too.

Tonight's dusk was by a painter of about twenty-two, who ended it on a slow blue that took the far bank with it. The terraces didn't clap for a whole minute, and then they did. I'd tell you the colours, but you'd have to see it.
Everything in {drum} is lit a little higher than it needs to be, the way some people talk a little louder. I've done a week's squinting in three days. I love it and I could never live here.
They sell seats for the painted dawn here the way you'd sell seats for a play, and the cheap queue starts at five. I queued. So did the painter, with a coffee, pretending not to listen to us.
There's a board by the platform listing what this year's rents bought back: the terrace lamps, two choirs, an extra hour of sunline. It's a Ledger for showing off, and everyone stops to read it.
People here swear you can pick {drum} out from a glide, because it glows. You can't, the quay lights all look the same, but I've stopped arguing because I'd like it to be true.

Everybody in {drum} makes the one thing it's famous for, or teaches it, or argues about how. I was allowed to help for an afternoon and got told off by a twelve-year-old, which I gather is the proper start.

Everything here has a maker's mark if you look: under a bench, inside a cup, on the hinge of the hall door. I found one on the ring counter's ladle. Somebody made that ladle for this drum, and I've drunk from it.
I've learned more with my hands in three days than in the year before, mostly how much I don't know. The teacher says that's the first thing the school teaches and the only one that lasts.
The workshops in {drum} keep their doors open, so the whole street smells of glue and planed bamboo and warm dye. I've been invited into four of them and given tea in all four.
People glide to {drum} for one thing and go home with it under their arm. I'm going home with a mend on my jacket instead, done while I waited, the stitches left showing on purpose.
A maker here has been re-gluing the same armchair for thirty years, a little each year, because its owner likes an excuse to visit. They had tea while I was there and argued about the arms.

{drum} is a steady drum: no Margin, no Ledger, a plain register by the platform and a guest flat the size of a cupboard. It's decent and doesn't make a speech about it. The Mill Hall stew is the same as ours, and I was happier to see it than I'll admit.
Guests can buy a Hollow hour here, so I bought one. It was the dearest hour of my year so far, and I spent it lying on the grass watching people three kilometres overhead eat their lunch upside down.
Nobody in {drum} has heard of {home}. They were kind about it, then asked if it was near {nb}, and when I said no they lost interest completely.
I ate jook at the Mill Hall with three retired back-crew women who talked about the stars as if they were old neighbours. I'm saving what they said for when I see you.

Gin is cheap on one side of the glide to {nb} and dear on the other, so everyone crossing carries the two bottles you're allowed. I carried two for a stranger today, which I'm told is entirely legal and very much expected.
Most of the raft is steady drums, someone told me, and here I can see why: nothing in {drum} is trying to impress me, and everything works. I slept eleven hours.

{drum} is crowded the way our hall is on Booking Day, except every day. I'm sleeping in a bunk that's someone else's in the afternoon, and they left me a note on the pillow: 'Welcome. Don't touch the green blanket, it was my mother's.'
People here share everything: rooms, bunks, Hollow hours, the one good knife on the corridor. I've never been offered so much by people with so little room to spare.
The Hollow's so rationed here that I got twenty minutes of it, at lamp-night, with what felt like half the drum. It was still the best twenty minutes of the week.

No guest-right in {drum}, so I'm paying a few kays a night for a bunk, and I'd pay double for the company. The woman in the bunk below has told me her whole life, and I've told her mine, which took less time.
There's a rota for everything here: the showers, the kitchen, the corridor's one bright lamp. I've been put on it, which I'm told means I'm liked.

On the glide people said thin drums are just overspent, as if that's the whole story. It isn't. It's mostly a lot of people being very patient with each other in very small rooms, and very good at noodles.

{drum} is counted. The Count is on every platform, people against shares, and while the stop lasts the children here are fitted at fourteen. Nobody hid it from me and nobody wanted to talk about it, and then at dinner a grandmother talked about nothing else.
It's quieter in {drum} than I expected, and kinder. The Count by the platform has come down a long way this year, and someone has drawn a small heart beside the number in chalk.

The kitchen by the platform still cooks the blight menu from the year the vats went down, and it's the best cheap food I've had all year. The cooks say they'll keep it when the drum reaches par. I hope they do.
A boy of thirteen asked me what it's like in a drum that doesn't count. I said about the same, only louder. He thought about that for a long time.
Anyone may glide out of a counted drum; it's posted at the platform in bigger letters than the Count. Almost nobody here does. I asked a woman why, and she said, 'It's ours. We're fixing it.'

Went up to the Hollow today and spent the first ten minutes with my head back, like everyone does. The far bank is three kilometres up and upside down, and a child on it was running with a kite straight at me.
At half a g my strides were so long I felt enormous. A boy of six overtook me in the same strides, laughing at me the whole way.
At the lake the dives take half again as long, so you have time to change your mind halfway down. I did. It didn't help.
At lamp-noon you can't look at the sunline, so everyone looks at the far bank instead. It's like watching a stranger's picnic from underneath.

Guests get an hour of the Hollow. I spent mine under a pear tree with a tomato from a stall, cut into four with a borrowed knife and shared with three strangers, and now I have three friends in {drum}.
I watched the dusk from the top terraces, where you weigh almost nothing. A girl beside me jumped the height of a house and came down so slowly she had time to wave.
I flew today. Along the axis it's like swimming in warm nothing; crosswise it's like being argued with. My teacher was nine, called me big aunt, and laughed every time I hit the net.
The whole Spindle opens at night and people fly the length of the drum with hand lamps. I went up at eleven, came down at three, and I don't think I said a word the whole time.
The trick crosswise is to aim wide, like throwing anti at spinball. I knew that. My body didn't, and my elbows have the net marks to prove it.
From the axis the whole Hollow is round you at once, near bank and far bank, every lamp of it. I hung there in borrowed sleeves and thought of you, which is not very original, but there it is.
Nobody tells you stopping is the hard part. You flap the wrong way, you turn over, and you arrive at the net backwards, to applause.

I saw the River today, through a Window behind the radiators. I've started this card three times. Pale gold, more of it than you'd believe, black places where the other rafts are, and everything in me and everything I own fell out of it.

They made us wait twenty minutes in red light for our eyes to wake. I was the only one there over eight who wasn't somebody's grown-up, and the girl beside me held my sleeve when the shutter opened. I think I held hers back.

A raft's edge crossed a star while I watched. It took most of an hour, and then the star simply went out, like a door closed very quietly in another room. The guide says the back crews bet on those. I would.
Someone told me the apple at a wedding is a picture of the River, and I didn't understand until today. At the next wedding I'm going to cry at the wrong moment, and now you'll know why.
The gallery is weightless, so you strap into a couch and the River fills the long window in front of you. A hundred and fifty people and nobody spoke, not even the eight-year-olds.

Eight hours on a sled behind the radiators, holding tools on lanyards with the whole sky over my shoulder. I signed for the dose: a real form, with a real number on it, and a crew lead who checked I'd read it.
The crew call the brown-violet at the edges of the River 'bruise', and once you've heard it you can't see it as anything else. I'm bringing the word home for you.

We chased an ammonia leak along the panel rows half the morning. It shows as a little glittering fan of crystals, very pretty and very expensive, and {name} swore at it steadily and then fixed it in four minutes.
The crews bet on when a raft's edge will cross a star, and they let me bet too. I won a cup of tea. I've never been prouder of anything.
Day {day} on the slow line. I've been upside down to the person I'm talking to for an hour and neither of us has noticed. Soup in a bulb, bread in a net, and I'm very happy.

I added a spoon of {drum}'s broth to the Galley stockpot today, which makes me part of the history of a soup that hasn't gone cold in living memory. It tastes of about sixty drums, and now a little of me.
Light home is {light} and getting longer by about half a second a day. I've started writing you a long letter, the careful kind, to be read once. This isn't it; this is to say it's coming.
The bungee hour is compulsory, 'or your bones sulk', says the line's oldest rider, who is twenty-six. I've done it every day. My bones are sulking anyway.
The Galley has a shelf of starter crocks: take a spoon, leave a spoon. I've taken from four drums I'll never see, and somewhere down the line someone's baking with ours.
We played a slow world in the Galley tonight, twelve of us, and for once there was no lag at all, because we were all a metre apart. It felt like cheating.
The board in the Galley ticks off a row of drums every twelve seconds. I tried saying goodnight to each one and gave up at about forty.
I took the express. A hundred and eleven kays, five days of my wallet, and I'll be there by tomorrow lunch instead of next week. Don't tell anyone how much I spent.
The express is quiet. Everyone on it is going to something that matters: a birth, a funeral, a lover, a job. I'm going because I wanted to, which the man opposite says also counts.

The ramp is thirty-four minutes at a full g, lying back, with the tail of the capsule for a floor. Then it lets go, and you're doing twenty kilometres a second and weightless, and nothing at all tells you so.
Stood by the express ramp for a long time today doing sums: five days of wallet for three weeks of my life back. Then I went and had noodles, which I think means I've decided to go slow.
{drum}'s ring counter does the best broth of the year so far: peppery, with something sour waiting at the bottom of the cup. I know what you'll say about ours. Say it anyway; I miss hearing it.
I paid half a kay for a tomato today and ate it slowly on the platform like a fool. It was worth it. Tell nobody.
Food comes under lids here like at home, and I'd stopped noticing until a man lifted his before the table was served and everyone looked at him. Some things are the same everywhere.
Had ramen at a counter in {drum} that the Crosswise Guide gives one apple-seed star: worth the glide. It was worth the glide. I'd have taken a cycler.
The Mill table's the Mill table anywhere, but every drum hides the Nine its own way. Here it's sesame and black vinegar, and it's almost nice. Don't let anyone at home hear me say that.
Ate an orchard apple today, a whole one, alone, which I know you're never supposed to do. I cut it crosswise first to see the star. Bad guest, happy guest.

A cook here makes black garlic on the waste-heat loop, six weeks in the drum's spare warmth, and it costs nothing because the heat was going anyway. I'm bringing you some. The Gate won't mind; it's very dead.
I'm {light} away by light now. Sometimes on a platform I count it out, from when I say something to when you could have heard it.
Out here nobody's heard of {home}. I described it and a woman said, 'Oh, one of those,' very kindly, and I've spent a week trying to work out which those.
On this side of the raft they eat the bread before the stew, not after, and look at me as if I'd been raised in a vat. I've been eating it after, on principle.
This is as far from you as I'll get: {light} by light. Every card after this one comes from a little nearer, and I'm already looking forward to them.
I met someone from {far} who'd never met anyone from our row. We swapped broth recipes like secrets, and both of us are sure we got the better one.
Homesick today, for no reason. The lid came off the stew in {drum}'s hall and for a second it smelled like ours, and that was enough. Back on the glide tomorrow.
Every drum has someone practising a flute at eleven at night, and every one of them sounds like the one through our wall. I've stopped knocking. I just listen.
Day {day}. Nothing's wrong. I just wanted you to have something from me in your hands.
I'd spend a whole express fare to sit at our table for one dinner and come straight back. I wouldn't, really. But I'd think about it all the way to the ramp.
Someone in {drum} has the same chipped cups as our hall, from the same old maker I suppose, and I drank from one and nearly cried. Silly. Tell everyone I'm fine. I am fine.
I miss the sound of home, which I didn't know had a sound. It's the lifts, I think, or the way our hall rings. Every drum rings differently, and none of them rings like ours.
Booking Day in {drum}: the beam booked flat, the Ledger read, and a feast paid for by a Quiet I wasn't even here for. They wouldn't let me pay. Three people told me how I'd have voted.

Flew the Long Flight with a block I met yesterday: thousands of hand lamps along the axis, a choir singing somewhere ahead in the dark, and me, crosswise, apologising to everyone. Best night of the year so far.
Knotnight in a stranger's block. I made bread by hand lamp and knotted the string round three jars, and one of them has our drum's name on the label now, in somebody else's larder.
The Passing: the hall sang to the other raft tonight and we all sat through the thirty-three minutes. Then the answer started, their voices in their own heliox, and nobody could say anything at all.
It was the Quiet here today: no worlds, no messages, everyone in the halls just talking. That's why this card is late. I talked for eleven hours and didn't know I had it in me.

I was in {drum} for a Homecoming. Not mine: a girl came off the glide into forty hand lamps and her whole table, and I stood at the back holding somebody's spare lamp and pretending it was a rehearsal.
Last leg. I'm {light} away and closing. Meet me at the ring, and bring everyone, and bring a lamp.
I've got the list of every drum written inside my jacket lining, and the broth notes, and one argument I'm going to win at the ring counter. See you on the platform.
Next glide is home. I've been weightless and heavy and half heavy for a year, and I think I'm ready to be exactly as heavy as I was. Leave the lamps on.
Day {day}. The board says {home} in two stops. I've changed my shirt twice, which is silly, because it's the same two shirts.
